speechtext: On motion of Mr. Demers (St. John and Iberville), House went into committee to consider the report of the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons for the purpose of revising Rule 51 of the House of Commons and Rule 49 of the Senate, and making them agree. (Votes and Proceedings of House of Commons, August 18, 1903.)

I beg to move :	.
That the report of the Select Committee appointed to confer with a similar committee of the Senate, for the purpose of revising Rule 51 of the House of Commons and Rule 49 of the Senate, he amended by striking out the words ' oyer the name and address of the solicitor for' the applicant,' in the 8th and 9th lines, and inserting in lieu thereof the following ' signed by or on behalf of the applicant, with the address of the party signing the same.'
This will make rule 51 read as follows :
All applications to parliament for private Bills of any nature whatsoever shall be advertised by a notice published in the 1 Canada Gazette.' Such notice shall clearly and distinctly state the nature and object of the application, and shall be signed by or on behalf of the-applicant with the address of the party signing the same. And when the application is for an Act of incorporation, the name of the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
proposed company shall be stated in the notice.	-	.
.This has the consent of the Senate. Amendment agreed to.
On section (a), subsection 4,
In addition to the notice in the ' Canada Gazette ' aforesaid, a similar notice shall also be published in some leading newspeper, when the application is for an Act to incorporate a railway or canal company. In the principal city and town or village in each county through which the proposed railway or canal is to be constructed.

On behalf of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), I beg to move the following amendment:
That at the end of the first paragraph thereof the following words be added :-
And if the works of any company (incorporated, or to be incorporated) are to be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, such intention shall be specifically mentioned in the notice ; and the applicants shall cause a copy of such notice to be sent by registered letter to the clerk of each municipality which may be specially affected by the construction or operation of such works, and also to the secretary of the province in which such works are, or may be located ; and proof of compliance with this requirement by the applicants shall be established by statutory declaration.
That is for the purpose of giving notice to municipalities interested when in any Bill it is declared that the work is for the general advantage of Canada.
I understand that this has also been agreed to by the Senate.

Amendment agreed to.
On section (b),
(b.) When the application is for the purpose of amending anv existing Act :
1.	For the extension of any line of railway, or of any canal ? or for the construction of branches thereto :-In the principal city, town or village in each county or district through which such extension or branch is to be constructed.
2.	For the extension of the time for the construction or completion of any line or railway, or of any canal, or of any telegraph or telephone line, or of any other works already authorized :-In the place where the head office of the company is, or is authorized to be.
3.	For the extension of the power of a company (when not Involving the granting of any exclusive rights) ; or for the increase or reduction of the capital stock of any company ; or for increasing or altering its bonding or other borrowing powers, or for any amendment which would in any way affect the rights or interests of the shareholders or creditors of the company :*-In the place where the head office of the company is situated.
All such notices, whether inserted in the ' Canada Gazette ' or in a newspaper, shall he published at least once a week, for a period of five consecutive weeks ; and when , published in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, shall

be in both the English and French languages ; and marked copies of each issue of all newspapers containing such notice shall be sent to the Clerk of the House, endorsed * Private Bill Notice ' ; or a statutory declaration as to due publication may be sent in lieu thereof.
Why not have that private Bill notice in duplicate ? The notice must be considered by the Senate as well as by the House of Commons.
The Senate have the same rule.
These are rules agreed to by the Joint Committee of the House of Commons and Senate.

Yes, but they are to be rules of the House of Commons. They are not rules of the Senate, though the Senate will have the same rule.
On proposed rule 51c,
No petition praying for the incorporation of a railway company, or of a canal company, or for the extension of the line of any existing or authorized railway or canal, shall be considered by the Standing Orders Committee, until there has been filed with the committee a map or plan, showing the proposed location of the works, and each county or district, through which the proposed railway or canal, or any branch or extension thereof, is to be constructed.

The applicants are obliged to furnish the Railway Committee with a map. We want to have a map before the Standing Orders Committee, in order that we may know that the notices have been given where they should be given. Of course, the same map can be used before the Railway Committee.
Resolutions reported, read the second time, and agreed to.

(a.) upon the completion of the work subsidized; or

The location also of such subsidized lines shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
6. subsidized, reasonable and proper facilities in exercising such running powers, fair and reasonable traffic arrangements with connecting companies, and equal mileage rates between all such connecting railways ; and the Governor in Council shall have absolute control, at all times, over the rates and tolls to be levied and taken by any of the companies, or upon any of the railways hereby subsidized.
7.	Every company receiving a subsidy under this Act. its successors and assigns, and any person or company controlling or operating the railway or portion of railway subsidized under this Act. shall each year furnish to the government of Canada transportation for men, supplies. materials and mails over the portion of the line in respect of which it has received such subsidy, and, whenever required, shall furnish mail cars properly equipped for such mail service ; and such transportation and service shall be performed at such rates as are agreed upon between the minister of the department of the government for which such service is being performed, and the company performing it, and, in case of disagreement, then at such rates as are approved by the Governor in Council ; and in or towards payment for such charges the government of Canada shall be credited by the company with a sum equal to three per cent per annum on the amount of the subsidy received by the company under this Act.
8.	As respects all railways for which subsidies are granted by this Act, the company at any time owning or operating any of the railways shall, when required, produce and exhibit to the Minister of Railways and Canals, or any person appointed by him, all books, accounts and vouchers, showing the cost of constructing the railway, the cost of operating it, and the earnings thereof.
9. I have looked over the memorandum furnished me through the kindness of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with respect to the provisions of this Bill. House went into committee on Bill (No. 3) to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900.

The question of coping with the tendency to increase the electoral corruption in Canada is one the importance of which I need not dilate upon. Such corruption does exist to some extent, and to the extent to which it does.exist it is detrimental to the interest of our country, and threatens the integrity of our institutions. The Bill with reference to this question was referred to a special committee some weeks ago. That committee was composed of five members of the government side and four of the opposition side, and it entered upon its labours with a

sincere desire to report a Bill which would be serviceable to Canada and in the public interest. Such a thing as political feeling was not manifested in this committee in the slightest degree. Every member of the committee gave his best efforts to perfecting a Bill which we had reason to believe would be acceptable to the House and in the interest of the country. The committee had the aid in its labours of the Department of Justice. One of the officials of that department attended the meetings of that committee regularly, and acted as counsel in every legal matter. It had also the assistance of the law clerk of the House of Commons. The members of the committee were unanimous in their approval of the provisions of the Bill now submitted to the committee except on the one point, that one with regard to compulsory voting.
The provisions of the Bill as now submitted received the unanimous approval of the special committee, with the exception of the clause with reference to compulsory voting. We had the benefit during some of the sittings of this committee of the services of the Minister of Finance, and they were invaluable to us; and the feeling that characterized the members of the committee in their labours and at the conclusion of their labours, was most agreeable, pleasant and satisfactory, and gave augury, I trust, of the acceptance of this Bill by the House. The Bill we now proceed to commend to the consideration and the judgment of this House. If it is the opinion of the House that any other provisions of the Bill should be dropped, ol' course the committee is in the hands of the House in that respect, and it may be, from the fact that there was not unanimous concurrence on the part of the special committee with regard to the provision about compulsory -voting, that it will be prudent and desirable to drop that provision. I leave the House to consider that question. I will now describe very briefly the provisions of the Bill-. The first provision is with regard to compulsory voting, or penalty for non-voting. By a provision of the Bill, an elector failing to vote is disfranchised for a period of six years ; but if he is absent from the riding, if he is ill-
How do you disfranchise him ?
Prevent his voting for six years, he is not eligible to cast a vote for six years.
By what mode or manner ?

By the fact that he refrains from voting, and his name does not appear on the list. But as I was saying, if he shows that his failure to vote was due to absence, and that absence was not by design for the purpose of abstaining from
voting, if it was due to illness, if it was due to having voted in some other riding, then he is exonerated from the provision of the Bill. This provision, as I say, did not receive the unanimous approval of the committee, and that is the only provision which did not receive unanimous approval. Section 11 of the Election Act of 1900, is amended. The section as it stands on the statutes provides that :
The person to whom a writ is addressed, as hereinbefore provided, shall be the returning officer at the election to which such writ relates ; provided always, that if the person to whom the writ has been addressed refuses, or is disqualified or unable to act, the Governor General may appoint another person to be such returning officer.
This section is repealed, and the following substituted for the same :
Section 11. The writ shall be addressed to the sheriff or the registrar of deeds, or to one of the sheriffs or one of the registrars of deeds, for the electoral district or some portion of the electoral district for which the election is to take place, and he shall be the returning officer at the election.
2. If, from any reason, there is no sheriff or registrar to whom the writ can be addressed, or if the sheriff or registrar is disqualified or unable to act, or if any other person to whom the writ has been addressed refuses or is disqualified or unable to act, the Governor in Council may appoint another person to be such returning officer.
No more than one writ shall be addressed to the same returning officer at one time. The object of this provision is to place the office of returning officer in the hands of sheriffs and registrars so far as that may be possible, and I think this is a provision which will commend itself to the judgment of the House. These are officers of high standing, -not likely to he influenced by political considerations, and corrupt motives in making tlieir appointments will of course be absent. The next change in the Bill is an amendment of section 13. A subsection is added to this as follows :
Any person who, when he is disqualified under the provisions of this or of any other Act, acts as returning officer, election clerk, deputy returning officer or poll clerk, shall be disfranchised for a period of seven years, and shall be guilty of an indictable offence, and shall be liable to imprisonment, without the alternative of a fine, for a term not exceeding twelve months and not less than six months, with or without hard labour.
A section is added to section 12 as subsection (i) :
Persons other than sheriffs or registrars of deeds holding any public office either Dominion or provincial

Are also debarred from acting as returning officers. Section 21 of tbe Act is amended by inserting after tbe word 'lists' in tbe third line thereof, the words ' and of an abstract of the offences and penalties under this Act.' This is the result of a previous

Then two new subsections are added :
(j.) Every employer of labour who, within the ninety days next preceding a general election, pays any employee his wages or salary in a pay envelope, or puts up or otherwise exhibits in the shop, factory, establishment or place where his employees work, or in any place adjacent thereto, any handbill or placard, upon which pay envelope, handbill or placard is written or printed anything which contains any threat, expressed or implied, intended or calculated to influence any such employee in the exercise of his franchise at such election, or which contains any notice or statement that the wages or work in such shop, factory, establishment or place will be affected by the success of any candidate of any political party, or by the success of any political party ;

Every person who, being an officer or employee of Canada or of any province thereof, directly or indirectly pays or promises to pay, or induces or compels, or attempts to induce or compel any other person to pay or promise to pay, or who receives from any other person, any subscription, contribution, or assessment for political purposes, or who prepares or makes, or takes any part in preparing or making, any political assessment, subscription or contribution ;
And every person so offending shall be disfranchised for a period of seven years and shall be guilty of an indictable offence, and shall be liable, if he is a returning officer, election clerk, deputy returning officer, poll clerk or other officer engaged at the election, to imprisonment, without the alternative of a fine, for a term not exceeding twelve months and not less than six months, with or without hard labour, and, if he is any other person, to a fine of not less than one hundred dollars and costs and not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, to any person who sues therefor, or, in default of payment of such fine and costs, to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months and not less than three months, with or W'ithout hard labour.
The next and last provision of this section is one which will be of interest to the members of this House and to the country :
Provided always, that the actual personal expenses of any candidate, his expenses for actual professional services performed, and bona fide payments for the fair cost of printing, advertising, bill posting and rent of halls or rooms for public meetings, or for meetings of committees, or for expenses for speakers at public meetings, or for canvassers or organizers-which canvassers and organizers in electoral districts situate wholly or in part in cities shall not exceed ten, and in other electoral districts shall not exceed three-shall be
held to Be expenses lawfully incurred, and the payment thereof shall not be a violation of this Act.
Section 108 has added to it the following as section 108a, in addition to the provisions preceding.
108a. A person offending against any provision of the next preceding section shall be a competent witness against any other person so offending, and may be compelled to attend and testify on any trial, hearing, proceeding or investigation : provided that if such person has answered truly all questions which he is required by the court to answer, he shall be entitled to receive a certificate of Indemnity from the court, which may be in the form FF, and the testimony so given shall not thereafter be used in any prosecution or proceeding, civil or criminal, against him.
2. A person testifying and obtaining a certificate of indemnity shall not thereafter be liable to any action, indictment, prosecution or punishment for the offence with reference to which his testimony was given, and may plead the said certificate of indemnity accordingly, in bar of such action, indictment or prosecution.
This provision is, of course, one of very great importance, and the friends of this measure rely largely on it to stamp out the evil of electoral corruption. It places the briber at the mercy of the person with whom he tampers ; it makes the business of bribing eminently unsafe. It is not a mere experiment for it has been tried in some of the United States and found to be effective. The objection was raised and discussed that there was a probability of blackmail being levied, but it is impossible to avoid the chance of blackmail where prosecutions may be made by a private person. In practice the plan has been found to be satisfactory and efficient. And the evil of electoral corruption by the purchase of votes at the poles has been stamped out.
Section 113 is also amended. Section 113 relates to the conveying of voters to the polls and the penalty and the disqualification of voters offending in this regard. The provision that follows is also one of great interest and one which will meet the approval of the House. It was fully discussed and it is admitted that it has been found impossible in practice to prevent the doing of that which this provision makes legal.
Section 113 is amended by adding the following proviso :-
Provided, however, that nothing in this section shall he held to make it illegal for any candidate or other person to hire bona fide for any purpose and for the ordinary and reasonable price, any horse, team, carriage, wagon, cab, sleigh or other vehicle belonging to, or in the usual and ordinary employment of, any regular cabman or livery man.
What is in section 113 ?

I shall read section 113. It is as follows :
The hiring or promising to pay or paying for any horse, team, carriage, cab, or other vehicle,

by any candidate or by any person on his behalf, to convey any voter or voters to or from the poll, or to or from the neighbourhood thereof, at any election, or the payment, by any candidate or by any person on, his behalf, of the travelling and other expenses of any voter, in going to or returning from any election, are unlawful acts ; and every candidate or other person so offending shall forfeit the sum of one hundred dollars to any person who sues therefor ; and any voter hiring any horse, cab, cart, wagon, sleigh, carriage or other conveyance for any candidate, or for any agent of a candidate, for the purpose of conveying any voter or voters to or from the polling place or places, shall, ipso facto, be disqualified from voting at such election, and shall, for every such offence, forfeit the sum of one hundred dollars to any person who sues therefor.
With this amended provision applying only to conveyances belonging to regular cabmen or liverymen, the committee were unable to see, after a full discussion of this matter, where any criminal intent or any consequences that would be corrupt in its character would follow the hiring on election day of the conveyances of a liveryman or cabman for the purpose for which they are uniformly and universally employed at every election. This simply makes legal what has been done with a great degree of impunity without such legislation.
Does this legalize the hiring of cabmen or liverymen during an election day ?
Yes, but it does not legalize the hiring of farmers' rigs or others than those of liverymen.
What happens in the case of a rural constituency where there are no cabmen and no liverymen ?
In such a case no rigs can be hired. If they could be hired you would have all of the farmers wanting to have tlieir rigs hired.
That legislation is for cities.

This legislation is for cities. It is in the judgment of the House whether it is proper legislation or not; it is in the knowledge of the House that in cities it is the universal custom to employ cabmen and this cannot be avoided.
Section 117 is also amended. Section 117 relates to voting by persons who are not qualified. The amendment is as follows :
Any alien or any other person, not being a voter, who resides outside of Canada, who canvasses for votes or works in any way to secure the election of any candidate, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and shall be liable to a fine of not less than one hundred dollars and costs and not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, or, in default of payment of such fine and costs, to Imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months and not less than three months, with or without hard labour.
We have had in elections in Canada the evil of touters and election workers from the Mr. CHARLTON.
United States who are brought into Canada and who travel up and down violating the election law'. But the day after the election or the night of the election they are gone beyond the jurisdiction of the Canadian courts. Under the provisions of this law they are prohibited from doing this, and by a provision to which I will refer later they can be arrested.
Then we have :
Form U in schedule 1 to the said Act, as enacted by section 12 ef chapter 16 of the Statutes of 1901. is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :
This is a provision with regard to compulsory voting. If the provision for compulsory voting is retained this wdll be retained ; if it is not this will be dropped. I do not know whether it will he necessary to read it. It is merely a provision for the person who is disfranchised in consequence of having failed to vote, securing his vote if his absence is unavoidable or for sufficient reason.
Section 131 makes provisions with regard to civil and criminal procedure ; with regard to the recovery of penalties and forfeitures and a new' section, which is added to is as 131a, is as follows :
If a person is charged with any Indictable offence under this Act, and it is feared that' he will endeavour to avoid arrest, It shall be sufficient to charge generally that he has committed an offence under ' The Dominion Elections Act,' without specifying the nature of such offence. The information in that case may b<^ in the form GG, and the justice receiving any such information shall thereupon issue a warrant in the form HH. Upon such person being arrested and brought before a justice, the justice shall state to him the particular offence with which he is charged and thereafter the case shall be proceeded with in the usual manner.
This provision enables a summary arrest to be made without specifying the nature of the charge for which the prisoner is arrested. These specifications will he made when the case comes before the justice of the peace. This law will enable the authorities to arrest such people as these workers from the United States or any person 'who is suspected of transgressing the provisions of this law. The mere fact that there is power to make such arrests, or the making of two or three arrests will have a deterrent and salutary influence and will also enable , the prompt administration of justice in the case of such offences. These are the changes and provisions in this amended Bill, and 1 repeat what I said at the outset, that with the exception of that referring to compulsory voting, they received the unanimous approval of the special committee. The gentlemen on that committee were thoroughly competent for the work they had to perform ; they were men wTho took a broad and critical view of all the questions discussed. These questions wrere discussed fully, with the utmost freedom and the greatest parti-

cularity. I do not suppose that a discussion of the character held by that committee could be excelled by a discussion in Committee of the Whole, or perhaps equalled ; because the members of the committee sat down quietly to the discharge of their duties, with a sincere desire to arrive at the facts and at a proper conclusion. They had no political purpose to serve ; they had no such thought in their minds. Their object was to perfect a Bill which would be beneficial and salutary to the Dominion of Canada, which would tend to cure evils of a growing and threatening character ; and- I commend this Bill to the judgment of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the promoter of the Bill has gone over its salient points, as proposed, we had better now take it up section by section.
What protection is provided for the ballot boxes after the voting has taken place ?
The same protection that exists at present. The election law of 1900 is not superseded.
There is no change, then, in that respect.
No.

Then, I want to state that I was subject to great difficulty at one time by the stealing of a ballot box, and 1 would like to have in this Bill some protection for the ballot box after it leaves the returning officer's hands until it reaches the place where the boxes are to be opened, in case of a recount. The ballot box I speak of was actually stolen from the train in transit between Alberton and Summerside. I would ask the hon. gentleman to insert a clause in the Bill protecting the ballot boxes from the time they are opened until the recount takes place before the judge.

I am sure that the members of the committee would be delighted to accept any suggestion to further perfect the Bill. However, at this stage of the session, perhaps it would be wise to accept the Bill if it is good as far as it goes. We shall have another session-at least, I venture the supposition that we shall -and there will then be time to add other provisions which my liou. friend and other members may suggest. If we accept the Bill as it is presented to-day, I think we shall make a long step in advance, and shall be in a better position to consider other proposed amendments than we should be if no action were taken with regard to the Bill at the present time.

I think that in the Act referring to Prince Edward Island the postmaster is required to place in the post office a list, or something of that kind.
Mi-. CHARLTON. He receives a bundle of lists, which he is required to hand out to the electors who come for their mail.

Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER, If it is the general wish of the committee to have a general discussion on the first clause, I am perfectly willing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am governed by the rules of the House, and I think
As the Gaelic of my hon. friend from Iberville was rather imperfect, I appeal to him to use the tongue we are accustomed to.

I shall be happy to oblige my hon. friend, although I am afraid I will be still more imperfect in my English than in what the hon. gentleman describes as my Gaelic. Some of the members of the special committee appointed to consider this Bill were of opinion that we should not adopt this clause providing for compulsory voting. Since then I have had occasion to consult my colleagues, and I believe that public opinion, in the province of Quebec at least, is opposed, at the present, to any such law. As some of the newspapers have justly pointed out, we are, by this clause, taking a very peculiar position. Because a man did not vote at one election we are going to punish him by disfranchising him for six years. We say : Because you did not vote this year, you will not vote for six years to come. That is not the proper way to teach people to do their duty, if we consider it is their Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
duty to vote. The question then presents itself : How and when is this man to be put back on the list after he has been disfranchised, and at whose expense ? If a man has not had the right to vote during six years, the probability is he will for ever be precluded from voting. I consider this a very harsh measure to adopt. In my opinion, a man should not be obliged to vote. There may be many reasons why he should not. The candidate who represents his opinions may be opposed by one of his relatives, and so on, and there may be delicate reasons, which everybody will approve, why a man should not vote. And if he went to the polls he would be suspected. It is not allowed to an English jury to refuse to say whether a man is guilty or not, but I am told that a Scotch jury may do so by returning the verdict ' not proven.' In many cases people should be at liberty to say that they do not know for whom they should vote. We are told that a man may be obliged to go to the polls, but he need not vote, because he can throw a blank ballot into the box. In my opinion, no one should be obliged to resort to such a subterfuge. No man should be compelled to make the pretense of doing a certain thing. If a man goes to the polls lie should vote, but he should have the right of deciding for himself whether he shall go or not.

This section is no doubt the most material in the whole Bill. I can see a good many things in it which should lead the majority of the committee to report favourably on it. It is probably a fairly good compromise with compulsory voting. I do not think it Is properly called ' compulsory voting,' but it is a pretty fair compromise. To that extent I endorse it. We have the right to insist that a man should vote when able to do so ; and if he does not take sufficient interest in public affairs to vote, in all probability lie would not be' much damaged by having his franchise taken from him ; and those who refrain from voting for corrupt purposes, as is frequently the case, should be disfranchised. It would appear to me that the committee have not studied this matter as deeply as they might. For Instance, there is no extension of the hours in which the polls are to be kept open, as there should J>e, if yon are going to make voting compulsory. At present the hours are too restricted. Either you should lengthen the hours or make the polling day a holiday. Nor should it be a sufficient reason to take before a judge that a man did not poll bis vote because he was at work or that he had not time during dinner to cross the city to cast his ballot. When we make compulsory voting a law, we should not allow it to be evaded by trivial excuses. There are, no doubt, many excuses which, while they would not appeal to those interested in elections, would he sufficient to prevent those who are not keenly interested from

going to any extra trouble. Take tbe city of Winnipeg during ani election in the/ middle of January. It is quite a feat for a man to go and cast a vote in the middle of the day, or between nine and five. The only time the workingmen really have Is after six o'clock at night. Men living a quarter of a mile away from their work, with the temperature twenty to forty degrees below zero, are not very much disposed to lose time in going to the polls ; and if we are going to make voting compulsory, we will have to extend the hours. I am decidedly in favour of the principle of compulsory voting, but I am not in favour of it with the restricted hours of voting that we have at the present time.

I cannot see my way to support the proposition. I think the people themselves are the best judges as to wlie-they they should vote or not. The amendment provides that a man who does not want to vote shall go to a judge and show that judge that he has ' good and sufficient reasons ' for not wanting to vote. If you carry that out, then, so far as the North-west is concerned, you will need to employ a good many more judges. And what are * good and sufficient reasons '? Supposing one member of a man's family is sick is that a reason that he could give before a judge to relieve him from the penalty of being disfranchised. Suppose a man is quarantined with his family on account of contagious diseases would that be * a good and sufficient reason ' ? Suppose a man has religious convictions against voting
Oh, oh.

Yes, there are hundreds of men who do not vote on account of their religious convictions. And among them are first-class citizens. There are many of them in my own constituency. They are among the best citizens we have.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) allow me to ask him a question? If these persons are disfranchised on account of religious conviction, why should ' they want to get on the list ?

The list in the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fowler's) part of the'country is not the same as in ours. In his province they have a printed list prepared at a certain time by a revising officer. But in our country we have nothing of that kind, but lists made up by enumerators about ten days before the election. And these enumerators put on the list every person who is a citizen and entitled to vote.
That is the way the lists are made in Ontario.

A man's name may be on the list but he exercises his own judgment about voting. Our election laws seem to have worked very well for the last thirty years or so. and I do not think any good 425J
reason has been given for disfranchising a man at one election because he did not think it well to vote at a previous election or because, for any reason, lie did not go before a judge and give ' good and sufficient reasons.' It either disfranchises him or puts him to a lot of expense and trouble.

As a member of the committee to whom this Bill was referred, I may	.say that there was
no clause of it to which we gave more attention than to this one. The committee tried to do their duty in the amendment of our election law as well as they could at the time at their disposal. It was late in the session before we got to work on this Bill, but when the matter was placed in our charge we worked faithfully and did our best to make such a Bill as would commend itself to the House. On the subject of compulsory voting we took a different view from that of some hon. gentlemen with regard to the fundamental question of the right to vote. While the right to vote is a privilege, it carries certain responsibilities, and one of these responsibilities is that the man shall exercise the franchise that is given him. It is not for the man who enjoys his privilege to say whether he shall exercise it or not. The committee felt that he should be obliged to fulfil the duties and accept tlie responsibilities of citizenship. Moreover, we felt that to make such a law as is here proposed would be to take a long step towards putting down the bribery which, we must all admit, is altogether too prevalent throughout this country. That is the object. And we made the period of disfranchisement six years so as to cover the next election. What the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has said with respect to lengthening the hours of voting might be necessary in cities, I can quite understand that. But it would not be necessary in rural constituencies, which of course, are the great majority of constituencies throughout Canada. That is a matter for this committee and the House to provide for by any further amendment which they may deem necessary. I think that subject was referred to in our committee, but we did not feel that we had much time to consider the distinction. The provision might easily be made covering the city constituencies, so that workmen would not be prejudiced by this clause. It seems to me that this could be very easily worked out. If a man does not vote there is no necessity to take any steps. If his name is upon the list it is tlie right of any person at the time of tendering his vote to object to the vote, and then he must take the oath. The point is covered by the oath and a penalty is imposed by this section. Any person representing either political party at the arranging and making up of the lists can object to a man's name being put on the list on the ground that he had not voted the previous election. There is no difficulty in arranging the matter.
Are not the lists arranged by the provincial authorities ?
I admit that that is a point to be considered. We ran up against that contention in the committee.
That is the knock-out.

It is a difficulty so l'ar as the making up of the list is concerned, but not so far as voting is concerned. Any one can object to a man voting. The hon. gentleman from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) does not know what a knock-out is. So far as the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) is concerned, he tells us that there may be persons whose religious convictions may prevent them from voting. Well, how are they injured by being left off the list or refused the right to vote ? Unless we assume that these persons are going to change their convictions between one election and the next.
Something might arise to cause them to change.

If so, then let them wait a little longer, until the next election, and then they will be able to vote. The principal idea that governed the committee with regard to the matter was to get at bribery and corruption, and we thought that if men were compelled to go to the poll there would be less object in attempting the bribery that is sometimes attempted. We felt that the privilege of voting carried with it the duties of citizenship, and that it was right to compel these persons to vote who, from indifference or any other cause refused to take part in the public work of the community.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) a question. Provision has been made in the case of illness on the part of a voter. But suppose that some member of a man's family is sick ; suppose that one of them is dead. Must the man then be disfranchised ?
That can be explained to the judge.

Well, he will have to go to the judge and explain ?
Mi-. CHARLTON. It will cost him nothing ?
It will cost him his time.

Well, suppose a man's name is left off the list, he has to go to the judge to get it on. This is not a singular hardship. You cannot make any general rule about anything without having individual cases in which the law seems to operate harshly.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is legislation run wild. That may be thought too strong language. If the franchise is a privilege I cannot quite understand how you can compel a man to

use his privilege. But this compulsory voting does not seem to me to be consistent with British right and liberty, and I for one am against bringing in legislation of this kind. I may be too young a member of this House to be quite justified in declaring my opinion so bluntly, but it seems to me that legislative bodies sometimes forget that there is a possibility of over-legislating. I think that if a Bill were brought in to stop such a thing as canvassing in an election, you might do some good. But merely to make laws against corruption that are easily broken will not put a stop to corruption in our politics. When it is possible for men to be coerced into voting for individuals and at the same time, the voting is compulsory, I think it is legislation run wild, and, I for one strongly object to such a proposition. I think it is one that should be struck out, and let us go on with some other work that will be more advantageous to the country.

The hon. gentleman talks about liberty, yet he is willing to restrict men from canvassing. I do not think that compelling a man to vote is half as much a restriction of his personal liberty as' to refuse him the privilege of eanvassiug. Yet the hon. gentleman talks dbout legislation running wild. He forgets that while we Jiave the privilege of voting, that privilege carries with it duties and responsibilities.
The privilege of canvassing also.
I merely made that suggestion, without intending to lay it down ns a principle.

The committee endeavoured to overcome a difficulty that prevails in all election campaigns. The idea no doubt was to compel a man who holds back his vote to about five minutes to five, to go and poll his vote in good time. Ai the same time, I think the thing is practically impossible ; you cannot carry out compulsory voting. It is an ideal system, over which there has been considerable discussion, yet I think any one who has had experience in election matters will know that it is utterly impossible to carry that out. Take for illustration the case of two candidates, both of whom we will suppose happen to be undesirable men.	A man may say to his
friends, or he may say to himself :	I am
not going to cast my vote for either of these men ; they do not come up to my standpoint of what a candidate ought to be, and I am not going to vote for either one of them. But this law compels him to go to the polls and vote ; if he does not, he becomes a criminal. Further than that, reference has been made to the fact that in the North-west Territories, and the same may be said of other parts of the country, there are in certain places men of peculiar religious convictions who do not desire to

poll their vote. We know also that there are the Brethren who hold religious scruples against voting, and some of them do not vote. I understand that in the North-west there are also a number of Mennonites who hold that it is wrong to vote. Now, I think, as men have a right of individual action, this parliament has no right and has no power to compel a man to go forward and record his vote. I think every citizen of this Dominion, or anywhere else, has the individual right to do as he likes to a certain extent. I do not agree with the idea that the right of citizenship carries with it the duty of voting. I agree to some extent with what has been said by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Mac-pherson), that this is a privilege offered to a man to exercise if he desires, or to refrain from exercising if he feels so disposed. But I do not think it is within the province of this parliament to compel a man to go forward and record his vote against his will. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that in this respect the less we interfere with what might be called a man's privileges, so far as election matters are concerned, the better will we be consulting the interests of the community at large. There is such a thing as legislating too much. It is all right to legislate against improper practices in any respect that will be detrimental to the welfare of the community, but in respect to this particular form of legislation, I am satisfied that it will do infinitely more harm than good. You cannot imagine, if you were to carry out this principle, what might be the consequences in a community where, w*e will say, 40, or 50, or 100 men do not choose to go to the polls and record their votes. I do not know whether the Liberal party, I am very doubtful whether the Conservative party, would feel disposed to prosecute those men because they did not vote. If they did prosecute them, you can easily imagine the dismay that would exist in that community. I am satisfied that the outcome would be infinitely worse than if you left them to do as they please.
There is no penalty except the loss of the right to vote, they are not prosecuted.
Very true, but in the eye of the law a citizen becomes a criminal if he does not vote, and is punished by being disfranchised.

I think the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) and the hon. member for West Huron, both misconceive the legislation, as I understand it. The effect of this legislation is that if any voter, entitled to vote in Canada, chooses to say :	I do not want the privilege of
voting, and therefore I wont't vote-you disfranchise him for six years. Now this man who refrains from exercising his right to vote is not being punished at all, he is only being told :	Since you have said that
you do not want to vote in this election, we won't let you vote for six years to come ; but if you change your opinion within the six years, you will be allowed then to vote. There is no punishment about it, there is nothing except an enforcement of the man's own exercise of his privilege to refrain from voting. He has now the privilege of voting and he says he does not care for that privilege.	1

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? He says he is not punishing the individual. Now is it not doing a great wrong to the individual who, on one occasion, will not vote, if the government compels him for six years after to refrain from voting ?

Well, if this man whom my hon. friend is so anxious to protect wants to exercise the privilege of voting, he has it; in his own power to decide whether he wants to vote or not for six years. He knows the law, everybody in Canada is presumed to know the law ; and if a voter knowing that law does not vote, and knows that he cannot vote again for six years, why, he decides his own case, and you are practically confirming him in his decision. He decides his status for six years, decides it deliberately, with all the knowledge of the consequences. He says to the government :	I declare, by staying
away from the polls, that I do not want to vote for six years. You allow him to decide his own case, and what harm are you doing him ? You cannot say to the Speaker of this House that you do not want to vote on such and such a measure, when you are present. Every man here has to vote unless he is paired. It is a duty to the state, here as in a political election. I am not so sure, however-and I do not want to be misunderstood-that the section as drawn will carry out the object in view. But I think that we can agree upon the principle that when a voter who declares by not voting that he does not want to~ vote, when he knows that by so doing he cannot vote for six years, we are not depriving that indivi-duai of a privilege by disfranchising him, we are in fact giving him the highest privilege we can give to any man, and that is the privilege of deciding the extent of his own rights for the next six years.

Supposing two undesirable candidates are before the electors, and that a clergyman, for instance, did not choose to cast his vote for either of them, thinking they were both undesirable, would the hon. gentleman disfranchise him for six years ?

I have always found that when there were two candidates there was one who was less undesirable than the other-if the hon. gentleman can understand that-and I say it is the duty of the clergyman, or

135S0
of any other elector, to select the least undesirable and to vote for him, that is, if he desires to vote at all. In my own county we have had to select between men neither of whom would be our choice if we had the right of nomination. The voter has got to come to a conclusion as to which of the two men, on all the evidence that he can procure, is the least desirable, or the most desirable, and he has to give the best decision he can. I think anything that will increase the responsibility of a voter will by so much advance the welfare of the general community ; and if we teach voters that a responsibility attaches to them, that they are under an obligation to inquire into the qualifications of the candidates and to vote for the least unfit-that is if they deside to vote at all-we will be legislating in the right direction. Let the voter pause before he decides not to vote, let him inquire a little further into the qualifications of the candidates, and perhaps a day or two later he will come to the conclusion that he does see a distinction between the two men, and that he will vote for the one he thinks the better man. I think a provision of this kind will cause the elector to be more careful, to search into the qualifications of the candidates with more care, and in that way the effect will be beneficial.

I agree with what the hon. member for King's, N. B. (Mr. Fowler) has said that voting is a privilege or duty. But who is to be the supreme judge of the exercise of that privilege or duty-is it the parliament or the individual ?
The individual.

Then you cannot prevent him. I believe that he ought to be the judge of the exercise of that privilege and duty, and if he should be the judge of both, he ought to be allowed to stay at home if he thinks he is performing his duty thereby better than, under the compulsion of this parliament, going out and voting. Who is to be the final judge of privilege and duty V There is such a thing as parliament taking legislation into its own hands that it has no right to take, and I think it would be a grave mistake for this parliament to say that a man, who perhaps has studied a question just as much perhaps as this parliament has, shall exercise his franchise although he says that by refraining from exercising the privilege of voting he is serving his conscience better than if he went out and voted for one or othdr of the parties. He should be the supreme and final judge of that. A question may come up which may be a political question. It may be a direct party question. On one side we may take one view and on the other side there may be a different view. There may be an hon. gentleman on the opposition side who says that he agrees with the view which the government take, and there may be an hon. gentleman on the
government side who may say that he does not agree with it. What are these men to do ?
They will be whipped into line.

Not at all. A time comes in parliament on one side or the other when a man simply says :	I will abstain
from voting. I cannot vote against my party, but the fact that I disagree with my party in regard to the view which has been enunciated by it does not make it necessary that I shall sever my connection with my party.

Then the hon. gentleman's argument is that a member representing the people is doing his duty by refraining from voting ?
Mr. FRASER, That gentleman as a representative of the people, must be the judge of what his duty is. I would like to see you introduce an Act into this parliament to provide that every man who is in Ottawa must vote or otherwise he cannot be a member of this parliament. There would be no difference between that and saying that a man who did not vote at an election should be deprived of his vote for six years. I remember a vote not long ago when a number of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House were glad to go out of this House and refrain from voting. They had a right to do it. I have known occasions on this side when hon. gentlemen felt it their duty not to vote. In any case it would be dangerous to say to a member of parliament :	You must vote.
If lie is in his seat he accepts the responsibility of doing so, but he may abstain from voting. If you say to a man, you must vote or you lose your privilege, I venture to make the assertion that you will make a number of people in this country worse citizens than they are to-day. You cannot drive men. There is nothing like individual liberty in the world. It is the only thing that makes for stable government that a man shall be the judge as to whether he shall vote or not.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that increasing the responsibility of the citizen degrades citizenship ?
Mr. FOWLEIt. Quotation.

We never say very mucli that is new, and if some bon. gentlemen understood that, they would not be so proud of what they do say. Feeling that, 1 would be very loath to say that because a man did not conscientiously think that on a given occasion he should vote he should therefore be told that he is not a good citizen, and that he cannot exercise that privilege. We do not cease visiting our friends because they may do something that we think they ought not to do. I do not think we should interfere with the liberty of the individual to decide for himself whether he is best discharging the duties of citizenship by voting or refraining from voting.
Hon. Mr. I1AGGART. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) seems to have forgotten the object of the Bill which is now before the committee. The statement of the hon. Minister of Finance (ITon. Mr. Fielding) and admittedly of every person in this House is that corrupt practices have been committed in the different ridings of this country, which both parties have resolved to Stamp out, What principle (is it most necessary to apply for the purpose of doing this ? The committee have applied, as a first principle, that of compulsory voting. That will do something to prevent the crime of corruption, if it does nothing else. But, I think they would have made it more effective if they had added another clause to the Bill-I know I differ from the great mass of the members of this House in reference to this-and that is a clause providing for open voting. If a man receives a bribe for depositing his vote his neighbours know what his convictions are, and he is ear-marked if he votes against his convictions. This would be a means of preventing that crime. There are only two ways of preventing bribery and corruption, and they a re by adopting the principle of open voting and compulsory voting. Talk about the liberty of the individual ! How is it infringing upon the rights of conscience to say that a man shall go up to the poll and deposit his vote ? There arc; lots of people who do not exercise their franchise, and who have not the right to do it. The party who has the right is the delegate of all the others, and if that right is delegated to him, he should exercise it. If no candidate is acceptable to him, he has the right to nominate a man who is acceptable to him. He has the right to vote, and the community have the right to expect that he will exercise the power which they have given him, because where there is power given to him it is his duty to exercise it. I have heard that principle advocated by perhaps the ablest Liberal who ever sat in
this House-Hon. Edward Blake. It has been advocated by Liberals in every section of the world. I think it is the correct principle, and I think the time has arrived in this country to compel every man, for the sake of decency in elections, for the sake of preventing bribery and corruption to exercise the right which parliament has conferred upon him. If the system of enfranchisement under the Act is not correct, let us have a correct one, but let us adopt the principle of compulsory voting, because It is one of those principles that will do more than anything else to prevent the crime of bribery and corruption.

There is just one point in favour of the motion under discussion to which I wish to refer, and that is that more people are bribed to stay at home and refrain from voting than are bribed to vote. If they were compelled to vote then they would not stay at home, and if they went to the polls they would naturally vote as they felt. That is why I think that this clause is a step in the right direction. As for the charge that a man is injured by being compelled to vote it seems to me that he is only doing his duty by voting. Everyman who is enlisted as a soldier is compelled to take arms to fight his country's battles and here is a duty, the duty of preventing bribery, corruption and bad government, more serious than any that a soldier was ever compelled to perform. We want to turn out bad governments, we want to put down any bad thing in the government. We want to destroy everything that is bad in this country and it can be done only through the ballot box. I think it is right that every man should be compelled to vote and to register his name personally previous to the election in the section where he lives. It costs the municipalities hundreds of thousands of dollars to get people on the voters' lists. I heard it said only yesterday in the House that the lists were not prepared. The lists should be ready every moment. Every man should be compelled, as I have said, to register his vote just as he is compelled to register the birth of his child, the death of his father or a marriage ceremony. If the man is capable of walking he should be compelled to register himself; if he cannot walk he is able to talk and he should depute some one else to register for him. The enormous expenditure of putting people on the lists should be undertaken by this government. Not only should it be a duty to vote but there should be some one of the right sort for the people to vote for. It so often occurs that we have not the right men before us and so we are obliged to vote for a poor Liberal or Tory when we otherwise would not. You are obliged to vote either for a Grit or a Conservative when in nine cases out of ten, if you had your will, you would not do so. You are

obliged to vote for one of them simply because you have put a barrier in the way of an honest man being a candidate. You fine him $200 if he does not get one-half as many votes as the highest candidate at the election. This is what you should remedy, that $200 fine if the candidate does not get half as many votes as the highest number polled by a candidate. Then you would more often have candidates of the right sort in the field; you would have a great many working men and you would have more men in the House of my stamp. I tell you it would be no injury to this country to have more men of my stamp here and everybody in this country knows that. But the Grits and Tories will bring out their candidates and the old man will be left at home.
Some lion. MEMBERS. No, no.

That is nothing to me. It is the people who will suffer, not me. Now Sir, I do not wish to make a burlesque of this, but I do hope that you will not amend this in the direction proposed but that you .will add another clause providing that no man will be allowed to contribute any money whatever to an election fund. That will do away with the bribery in this country.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

As section 2 involves considerable discussion, and the House is very thin, I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it be suspended, and that we pass to another.
On section 3-returning officers,
Mr. DAVIS, What is the object of having sheriffs and registrars act as returning officers ? ?
The object is to have some official person who would be absolutely responsible.
Somebody as far as possible removed from the political struggle that is going on.
I am afraid that whoever drew this section did not consider the matter very carefully, for there is no sheriff for an electoral district nor a registrar of deeds for an electoral district.

The second subsection covers that objection. It provides that if there is no sheriff or registrar to whom the writ can be addressed, or if the sheriff or registrar is disqualified or unable to act, another person may be appointed.
Every word in a section of a statute has to have a meaning, and there is no sheriff for an electoral district nor a registrar of deeds for an electoral district.
That can easily be amended by making it read : ' for the county in which the electoral district is situated.'
In the North-west Territories one sheriff would have jurisdiction over perhaps three ridings. For which would he be appointed ?

He could be appointed for any one of them. There is nothing more than a technical objection to any part of this section. The Minister of Justice is perfectly right in saying that you do not appoint a sheriff or a registrar of deeds for any area as an electoral district. But in the province of Nova Scotia there are seventeen counties which are electoral districts, and for each of which the sheriff is appointed. Therefore, you have the substance of the provision, although it may be necessary to make some slight correction in the words themselves.

In my own district there are four sheriffs and four registrars of deeds. I think this Bill ought to bav(e received more consideration than it has, and more perhaps than there is time to give to it. Perhaps it might be amended so as to read in this way : ' The writ shall be addressed to one of the sheriffs or one of the registrars of deeds for the county, district or territory served by him and comprised in the electoral district.' I am not sure but that would meet the case of the North-west Territories.
No, it would not. This provision would necessitate the sheriff leaving his office to attend to this business, and no ordinary person could fill his position.

Does he never leave his office for a day ?
Mi". DAVIS. It would take more than a day ; it would take three or four weeks. Suppose you addressed the writ either to the sheriff or the registrar of deeds, and he was not able to act. That would necessitate his notifying the government of that fact, and it would be necessary to issue another writ addressed to somebody else, and by that time it would be too late.
You have to find out in the first place whether the sheriff or the registrar can act.

For instance, in the county of Huntingdon, in the province of Quebec, the writ was issued to a gentleman, who held it for some time, when it occurred to him that he wanted to become a candidate himself, and he sent the writ back.

The objection raised is overcome at the present time by the fact that every returning officer has an election clerk, who does most of the work. It very often happens that the returning officer does not leave his home, while the election clerk puts up the notices and distributes the other necessary papers.

Hr. holmes. Wliat would be the advantage of appointing a sheriff in my county, for instance, where there are three ridings ? The sheriff would have one writ, and in the others the writs would be sent to reputable citizens. If you also had a registrar, one of the writs would be sent to him, which would still leave one to toe sent to a reputable citizen ; and if you sent one to a reputable citizen, why not send the whole three to reputable citizens ?

In a very large constituency, 500 or 600 miles long, it is absolutely necessary to have the returning officer as near as possible to the centre of the constituency. If the sheriff or registrar happened to be in one corner of it, he would not be a fit person to act as returning officer.
Suppose you had no suitable person in the centre of your riding, what would you do ? Would you get the nearest man to the centre ?
We will assume that within a riding there are people sufficiently intelligent to act as returning officer.

I know a case in which it became necessary for the sheriff to leave his own riding and become returning officer of the adjoining riding. There was apparently no impropriety in this, but it gave rise to a good deal of acrimonious discussion.

Suppose you had a sheriff living in Saskatchewan and you appoint him as returning officer in another riding. If the election resulted in a tie, the people would not like the casting vote to be given by one who was not a voter there.

The hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) inquired why, if it is necessary in any case to appoint some reputable citizen as returning officer, such citizens, not office-holders, should not be appointed in every case. The committee took the view that it would be in the public interest to appoint registrars and sheriffs, because they are removed from political influences and have the confidence of the public. instead of appointing gentlemen directly interested in the contest and who, in some instances, might not be as acceptable and as well fitted for the position.

I fail to agree with the hon. gentleman with regard to the nonpartisanship of sheriffs and registrars. In Ontario, at any rate, these men are as a rule active partisans. No man is likely to be appointed sheriff or registrar in Ontario unless he has been a strong, active politician, and he is not apt to forget his political prejudices even after he has assumed office. We have had experience in Ontario, in connection with Dominion elections, of the law requiring the sheriff or registrar of deeds to act as returning officer, and we
have also had that position given to other reputable citizens. To my mind the elections were just as fairly conducted in the one case as in the other. Besides, why should a man receive an appointment of this kind simply because he happens to be the custodian of an office ? I would prefer distributing the perquisites of the government more widely rather than have them go to the fortunate men who chance to have been appointed sheriffs or registrars. It seems to me we are proposing to give away too many of our powers. We have already adopted the franchise of Ontario and its voters' list. We practically have nothing to say now as to how our lists shall be made up and who shall be put on or struck off. We have gone further. Under the Redistribution Bill we have practically handed over to the Ontario government the formation of our constituencies, because if, in any instance the Ontario government should choose to organize a new county, that becomes an electoral district of the Dominion. Now we are proposing to hand over to file provincial government the appointment of our returning officers. Very soon we will have nothing left. Everything will be done by the provincial government. I think we should keep some of these powers in our own hands and have something more to say as to the constitution of the House of Commons than we appear willing to do in this Bill. Although I take no exception to the sheriffs and registrars, I think we Should allow the government to name whomever they like, whether sheriffs or registrars or private individuals.

I should think that the registrar would be the last man in the county to name as returning officer. If he has any duties, they call for his presence in his office all the time. If he has not, he has no business to be the registrar. The duties of the sheriff may leave him more free but, as far as my knowledge goes, in the west the duties of the returning officers are such as to take up the whole of their time and attention ; and if the sheriff has any duties to perform as such, he cannot at the same time act as returning officer. If there are exceptional circumstances or conditions, it is quite in order for the government to appoint a sheriff as returning officer, but to say he must be appointed is simply to say that, if he has any business to do as sheriff, he will have to neglect it while he is returning officer. In the constituency which I represent there are three sheriffs and two registrars. This constituency is to be divided into four, so that there will not be sufficient registrars or sheriffs to meet the requirements. In any ease, therefore, somebody else will have to be returning officer in place of the sheriff. It would toe very much better to leave the matter entirely in the hands of the government and let them appoint the sheriff where suitable, and somebody else where it is not suitable.

I should judge from the discussion and the opinion expressed by the Minister of Justice that this section does not receive that unanimity of approval which is desirable if it is to become law, and I am quite willing to drop it.

I do not consent to drop it at all. No reason has been advanced which should defeat the object of this section. That object is to take your returning officer from a class of persons in whom the people have confidence. If you do not have some provision of that kind, you will subject the government to the temptation of appointing ward heelers, and when irregularities take place they will be charged against the person who was selected as returning officer. The sheriffs in Nova Scotia are appointed by the local government and are Liberals for the most part, and they discharge the duties of returning officers fairly well. One or two have been charged with certain offences, and I am inclined to think that in one case the charge is well founded, but that was only one out of many instances. I believe it would be far better to name some class of persons from whom these returning officers are to be selected. So far as sheriffs are concerned, they have been doing this work in the province of Nova Scotia without any inconvenience so far as the public is concerned. I do not know about the registrars of deeds in the North-west Territories. But I do not think there would be any great difficulty in the province of Nova Scotia about having the registrar of deeds perform these duties. Because, in most cases, I believe, if not in all. they have some assistance in their offices and they could readily spare the time necessary to perform these duties. But it seems to me that in any case the intention of the committee is safeguarded perfectly well by subsection 2, which gives power to the Governor in Council in this matter. Wherever it is undesirable or inconvenient to appoint one of these officers the government must appoint some one else. But the government would have to make its choice from this class of officers or take a certain responsibility in going outside of their ranks, and it would be expected that if they did so, they would appoint men of similar character and men in whom the public would have confidence. That is the main point-that both political parties should have good reason to believe that the men selected will do what is right and just. You can do that better, it seems to me, by selecting your class, and then appointing, as far as possible, from that class.

I would draw the attention of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to the fact that if you are going to confine the selection to the sheriffs and registrars of deeds, then, as has been pointed out there would be a shortage in the North-west Territories; there are not enough of these officers to go round. If it is ne-Mr. OLIVER.
cessary to have public officials you might include the land agent, the homestead inspector, the fishery inspector and the forest ranger.

You might do a great many things which do not seem to be at all necessary. If an officer cannot be found among those specified in the Bill, the Governor in Council lias power to appoint some other person. There is no need to make an exhaustive list such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) has referred to. It is not even necessary that the appointment should be confined to government officers. But it is not only desirable but necessary that the person appointed should be one in whose fairness and impartiality all the people would have confidence.

So far as our part of the country is concerned it would be better to insert the name of the land agent instead of the registrar of deeds because the land agent can get out at any time while the registrar of deeds in many cases cannot leave his office.

On section 4,
Section 12 of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following paragraph :-
(i.) Persons, other than sheriffs or registrars of deeds, holding any public office, either Dominion or provincial.
What does this mean ?
This seems to depend on the previous section.

I was just about to suggest that. If the Bill goes through it will be necessary to amend the previous section by adding ' prothonotary ' as suggested for the province of Quebec. That is the law with us. Thus, the government is limited to the sheriff, the prothonotary and the registrar of deeds, and it might be as well to extend the list of officers from which the choice can be made. If section 3 is to be amended this one will need to be amended also.

We have in our province an officer called the prothonotary.
I do not know whther he is the same as the officer of that name in the province of Quebec.
He is the chief clerk of the court. I think it is the same office as in Nova Scotia.
Yes. I would not object to having the word ' prothonotary ' apply also to the province of Nova Scotia.
We could make it general. Of course it would only apply where there is a prothonotary.

Section allowed to stand.

a copy to each elector to whom any mail matter is sent.
What does that abstract mean ?
Any postmaster who wilfully neglects or refuses promptly to deliver to the electors any such abstracts shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding $50 and costs to any person who sues therefor :	provided, however, that this penalty
shall not be imposed more than once for each election at which such neglect takes place.
Now that returning officer gets those abstracts ; suppose that ten days have elapsed -there are only 30 days, I understand, between the issue of the writ and the election-supposing a week or ten days have elapsed before the returning officer sends out his abstract to the postmasters. Well, the postmasters In the rural districts get them, but the people may not come very often to the post office, and very often it is the younger members of the family who are sent for the mail matter. Therefore the postmaster will have no opportunity of delivering to the elector this abstract, whatever it means, and then he will be fined if he does not do it There might be an elector in the district who did not receive any mail matter regularly, or a fisherman who seldom receives any mail. I see a great deal of difficulty so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, and I imagine that no representative from that province could have been consulted by this committee.

I would like to know who is to pay the returning officer ? I think he receives the magnificent sum of $50 or $00 for his services. If you are going to impose this duty on him of sending out circular's to 10,000 electors, where is his pay to come from ?

I think hon. gentlemen are magnifying the difficulties in the way. Whether the wording of the Bill is sufficient to carry out the objects we have in view, may be a matter of debate, but the object is that every elector in Canada shall, immediately before the election, have his attention called to the provisions of the election law, so that he may not remain in ignorance of it. It is useless for us to pretend that people understand all about the election law; there are thousands of honest electors in Canada who really do not understand the provisions of the election law, and who would not wilfully violate it, but who do violate it because of lack of information. The object of this proposal, even if it costs a little money, even if you have to pay the returning officer more-the object is to make the electors acquainted with the law under which they are to cast their votes, and that is the whole object. If it has not been effectually accomplished by the wording of this Bill, then let us try to amend it in' some way, let us try and cause the distribution of this abstract containing in brief the chief provisions of the election law
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.)
under which a man is going to cast his vote ; I cannot see any difficulty in doing it.

I would ask the Minister of Finance to answer me this question :	In
the North-west Territories there are no printed lists in some places, and how is the returning officer to get possession of those lists so that he may carry out the law '? What is he going to do when some of the electors are 400 miles away, and there is no mail ?

I assume at once that under the peculiar conditions in the North-west Territories you cannot address this abstract. I assume that in the case of Prince Edward Island you cannot address it. But surely we can find some way by which to secure the public distribution of the abstract. That is what we are driving at, and if it cannot be done in this way, then take the best way available, in the North-west and in Prince Edward Island, for distributing this abstract.

Technically the position of the Minister of Finance is correct. But when he comes to the practical application of the provision he will realize the difficulty. Take for instance a riding where there may be 8,000 or 10,000 electors, in a rural constituency. You impose upon the returning officer tiie necessity of sending out circulars, putting them into an envelope and mailing them to 10,000 electors. Speaking from my own observation, I know that as a general rule the returning officer has all that he can attend to in the short time at ills disposal to see that the ordinary duties imposed upon him are properly carried out.
He may employ a clerk.

But suppose he does employ a clerk, as they do in the majority of cases, even then they find it very difficult to carry out the work imposed upon them.
I would call the attention of the government to a feature that is not in the Bill, but that we should consider, because it is the outcome of the last election. There were two or three additional [DOT] duties imposed upon the returning officer last year, for which no provision whatever was made for their remuneration. They were required to see that every ballot was numbered consecutively, and in my county they found it necessai-y in a number of instances to send thousands of those ballots from the town of Goderich to Stratford, in order to have them run through a numbering machine. The local office had not the equipment to do that work. AVhen they put in their bill for this work it was disallowed by the Auditor General, because there was no provision in the Election Act for paying work of that kind. There were two or three instances wherein the additional work and expenditure had been imposed upon returning officers for which no compensation was provided. I think the government ought to take that

into consideration, and to provide that where additional work is put upon the returning officer some further remuneration should be given him. The Auditor General himself told me in conversation at the time that there were a number of instances wherein the returning officers did not get what they should get for their services in doing extra work.

Apropos of .what the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) has said about the payment of returning officers, I have this remark to make : I look askance at all kinds of legislation which attempts to make me good, or attempts to make the public good. I do not think we can legislate along that line. But I want to call attention to this fact, that in our country we were obliged to send a deputy returning officer from Vancouver to Atlin, a distance of 1,500 miles, in the dead of winter last year. The personal travelling expenses of the returning officer were over $500, when he put in his bill to the Auditor General, after having paid this money out of his own pocket, the Auditor General refused to allow him any more than the $500 altogether. He was away two months. To my personal knowledge he is a straightforward man. He had to break the trail for 80 miles when the thermometer was irom 50 to 00 degrees below zero, and he had to remain in the hospital for two weeks after as a result of the exposure to which he had been subjected. Yet, the Auditor General, sitting in his well-furnished office, would only pay him the same rate that he pays men for serving in a similar capacity in the old settled ridings in Ontario.
