This matter has come under my own personal observation. I will not stand up for any man who is trying to loot the country, nor will I stand up for any man who makes use of his official position to keep back from a person that which rightly belongs to him.

I think it is proper in considering any proposition before the House that all features of it should be taken into account. While it may be said that this question of expense is only a detail in my humble estimation it is a detail that comes very close to the principle and certainly should be attended to. It seems to me that when the principle is being established the committee should be thoroughly aware as to what is involved in giving effect to the principle. The expenses being what they will be and the difficulties in giving effect to the proposition being what they will be, they should be provided for. In regard to tjhe requirement of sending information around to the electors to tell them how to cast their votes on election day, while I agree that it is very desirable that there should be the fullest degree of information, I think most of us will admit that in elections in the past there has been a fair amount of information current amongst the electors, that they have been fairly well informed as to how to cast their votes, and although they have not always marked their ballots, so the judges say, in the way in which they should have marked them, I think in many such cases the judges were rather in fault than the electors. The main reason for requiring this great expense to be undertaken is, first, the provision in the Bill providing for compulsory voting, and second, providing for the disfranchisement of any person who does not vote. That is the chief reason for the great expenditure which will be incurred in sending this information around and if that proposition is not adopted I thing there is no necessity for this clause at all.

I do not think there is very much necessity for sending that information to the electors because the newspapers usually print all the proceedings of the elections and nearly always tell every elector how to cast his ballot. They even mark it for him and they mark it for the candidate for whom they wish the elector to vote. But, there is one point I wish to make. We have discussed the question as to the personnel of the returning officer. I do not think the deputy returning officer has been mentioned and I think there should be a clause in this Bill saying who the deputy returning officer shall be and providing that hie shall reside not only in the electoral district in which the election takes place, but in the polling division. We had a great deal of trouble in the county where I live owing to a clause of this kind not being in the Ontario Act at that time. But the Ontario Act now provides that the returning officer must be a resident not only of the electoral district in which the election takes place, but in the polling division. Then no stranger can be brought into the section to manipulate the ballots or to commit any wrong which neither party are willing to see carried out but which when committed they are willing to palliate. I want the law so changed that a man cannot act as a deputy returning officer unless he is a respectable man and unless every man who comes to vote shall know who he is.
t
I am afraid that would prevent an election being held in some constituencies.

I agree witli the lion. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) on this question. I am of the opinion that any money expended by the parliament of this country to more fully educate the electors upon the law governing voting would be money well expended. It can not be very well argued, as my hon. friend from the west has said, that because this law will not be able to reach every elector that therefore the great mass of the people should suffer. I do not think that is a good argu-

ment. I think that in a large number of counties, in fact in all of the counties of old Ontario, it would be possible to carry out this law and I think that if a copy of the Election Act in so far as it may be obtained in a short, concise form, were placed in the hands of every elector it would be in the interests of the purity of elections. I think the clause should go still farther. I think that 200 or 300 extra copies of the law should be given to the candidates. In the election trials in Ontario, when the courts have investigated elections, many cases have been found in which the candidates themselves are entirely unfamiliar with the law of elections. If that be the case in many parts of Canada how can we expect the electors who are not taking such an active part in politics to be familiar with the law ? I agree with this clause and I approve of the expenditure of money for that purpose. I believe that the effect will be to purify the elections.

My hon. friend from *Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) had a difficulty about this question because he was unable to see from what source the expenses were to be met for the circulation of the abstract of the law, to furnish the returning officer with copies to send to the electors and with copies to be posted up. I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to section 21 of the Act, which says that :
Immediately after the issue of the writ of election the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall transmit to the returning officer a sufficient number of copies of the voters' lists, &e.
In the Bill we have a provision that :
Section 21 of the said Act is amended by inserting after the word ' lists ' in the third line thereof the words ' and of an abstract of the offences and penalties under this Act.'
So that it will be the duty of the clerk of the Crown in Chancery to send the lists to the returning officer and to send him the requisite number of copies of the abstract of the law for circulation. That difficulty then is overcome.
Does it say that the candidates themselves shall have a specified number ?

No, the provision is that the returning officer shall have a snffi-cient number to post up ten at each polling place and to furnish each voter on the list with a copy. It would be his duty to have these copies mailed and they shall pass through the mails free of postage. The only failure to provide fully for the requirements of carrying this provision into effect, perhaps, is the lack of a provision a6 to the remuneration of a returning officer. It was held during the discussion of this matter In the committee that this would be an incidental expense which the returning officer would be entitled to charge, that he would be entitled to charge clerical expenses, and for Mr. BLAIN.
the directing and furnishing of the envelopes if they were not sent by the department. As far as the objection raised by the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) is concerned tha!t it will be a job so difficult that the difficulties will be insurmountable, I do not think there is anything In that contention. It is a plain simple matter to receive a sufficient number of abstracts of the law and to mail these abstracts of the law to the persons whose names are on the lists.	It is a simple question of clerical force and clerical work. It can be accomplished in a very short period. There is no difficulty about it and as the Minister of Finance has forcibly said this is a provision of the utmost importance. My hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver! says that there is among the electors a fair amount of information regarding the law. I venture to say that at this moment not one-tenth of the members of the House would be able to tell us the provisions of the Election Law in regard to corrupt practices, practices prescribed by law ; and the amount of information on such subjects current in the country at large is very meagre. In multitudes of instances voters transgress and violate the law through ignorance; they do it innocently and if just before an election, when they would be most likely to read it, they had placed in their hands an abstract of the Election Law, the infractions of the law would not be so frequent as they now are. If this provision of the present Bill passes, the elector would see that the benefits of infringing the law by corrupt practices would be very small indeed. I am surprised that there has been any opposition to this feature of the Bill. It semed to me and to the other members of the committee that if there was one provision of the Bill which would meet with universal concurrence it would be this provision for bringing to the attention of the electors of this country the actual provisions of the law. Whatever might be the difficulties, great or small, that stand in the way of putting this feature into operation these difficulties should not be allowed to prevent the accomplishment of the object in view. The difficulty of addressing 7,000 or 8.000 or 10,000 of these abstracts to electors is one that could be easily overcome, and if a returning officer is not entitled to charge to incidental expenses the cost of doing this, then all that is required is an amendment to this Bill which shall provide for his reimbursement for this service.

The hon. gentleman has not had the same experience with the Auditor General as we have had in the west or he would not propose to charge this to incidental expenses. In a case in my riding he actually refused to pay for sending out the proclamation and the gentleman who published the proclamation in the newspapers for the benefit of the people at large, in order that they might have the information,

has not yet been paid. The hon. gentleman has not taken up the North-west Territory view of the case at all. I have shown that it is impossible to carry out this provision in the North-west Territories. If you want to scatter information broadcast among the electors, to my mind the proper way would be to provide for the employment of men at each poll on election day whose duty it would be to hand a circular containing this information to each elector before he entered the polling place.
Supposing the elector could not read 7

Then what would be the good of sending it to him by mail 1 If he received the circular three or four weeks before the election he would perhaps open it and throw it away and never look at it again. But if it was handed to him at the booth he would look at it and see what it was.
He has probably got his money before that.
The hon. member seems to know more about the money part of the business than I do.
We all do, be honest. We all do.

We are discussing a proposition now to place information into the hands and into the heads of the people witli reference to the election law and the best mode of doing that. The hon. member who has charge of the Bill suggests that the returning officer shall send out a Circular letter to every man whose name appears on the voters' list at a certain time. I take the ground that the better way to disseminate that information would be to hand out the circular at the polling booth on election day. So far as our part of the country is concerned, that is all you can do.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if there are no municipal lists in his part of the country ?
No, there are no municipalities.
What kind of voters' lists have you V

In our country we make up tile voters' lists ten or fifteen days before the election. The returning officer appoints enumerators. These go into each polling sub-division and enumerate the names of the people whom they find there who are, according to their judgment, entitled to vote. The enumerator has to post up in three conspicuous parts of the polling sub-division a copy of that list three days before the election. Then any person can object to any name that appears on the list or have his name added to the list if he is entitled to a vote. In that way the returning officer
has no lists; some polling sub-divisions are 300 miles inland with no railway communication and how is the returning officer to obtain the voters' lists in order to carry out the provision now under discussion V It cannot be done.

So far as the preparation of this abstract is concerned, the amendment proposed to section 21 makes provision for that, because the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is obliged to send a copy to each returning officer and it will therefore be his duty to prepare aud print this abstract. That is an answer to one objection which has been urged. As to the expense of sending them out I believe that you can have envelopes addressed at the rate of about $2 per thousand and if you had in a constituency say 5,000 electors the expense for that purpose would be $10. I do not think that the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) would feel himself oppressed with an expenditure of that kind even in each electoral division of Canada, because with 215 electoral districts, even if you expended $15 in each of them you would have a total expenditure of only about $3,500. That would be a trifling expenditure if the good results that are expected from the distribution of this information would be at all accomplished. Then, so far as the North-west Territories are concerned, it seems to me a very simple matter to deal with them in the same way as we are dealing with Prince Edward Island, and probably the same rule might have to be applied to Ontario cities, where lists are made up a short time before election day. You could send the abstracts to the post office and have a copy delivered to any man receiving mail matter and I would add to that an amendment that the abstract should be also delivered to any elector demanding a copy. I am sure that by that method you will get information into the hands not of every elector in Canada but into the hands of the greater part of them. It would be too expensive to undertake to put a copy into the hands of every man but you would accomplish substantially the object aimed at by doing something of the kind suggested. I regard it as important that the people should have in their hands an abstract of this kind. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said that not one-half the members in the House are fully acquainted with the portions of the election law dealing with corrupt practices. He might have gone further and said that not ten per cent of the members and not fifty per cent of the lawyers in the House could tell you, without reference to the law what its provisions are. Under these conditions you can understand what an extremely vague idea of the provisions of the law exists in the minds of the electorate at large. I believe that this will be money well spent and that the proposal should receive the support of this House.

I have no objection to the distribution of information about the election law; we all agree that that is quite desirable, provided the expense is reasonable. The objection is that the provision which has been made for the distribution is not practicable and it requirts to be amended so as to make it practicable.
What would the hon. gentleman think as to the suggestion I made with regard to distribution in the North-west Territories ?

What is suggested for Prince Edward Island would very likely measurably meet the case. Any means that will tend to a general distribution of knowledge in regard to the election law is quite acceptable ; but it is not desirable that the provisions of that law should be such as in the nature of things cannot be carried out. This fact, which is evident to every one in the House with regard to this particular provision, has been shown to exist with regard to every section of the Bill which has come before the House so far ; and I submit that it is not fair to the House at this stage of the session to place before it a Bill which, however good the intentions of its promoters may be, evidently has not been carefully thought out in its practical application. The time we have lost on this Bill so far is something that we cannot very well afford at this stage of the session, and we are not getting any closer to a decision with regard to it. For my part, I would be bound to fight the provision with regard to compulsory voting to a finish. I would respectfully ask the House and the mover of the Bill to consider the situation, and to consider whether any good object is to be attained by forcing on the discussion on the Bill, which, with all due respect, has not been carefully thought out in all its details. With regard to the distribution of knowledge on the election law, it is not the man who does not know who transgresses the law ; it is the man who does know. That is no reason why everybody should not be informed ; but the danger to the state is from the man who knows too much rather than from the man who is not thoroughly learned in the law. It is the man who knows all about the election law who burns the ballots and makes trouble, not the man who does not know7 anything about it. He is likely to keep within what he does know.

There is another consideration with regard to Prince Edward Island. At the present time we find it difficult to get men to act as rural postmasters, the remuneration is so small ; and if you put greater obligations upon them and render them subject to a possible fine, I am inclined to think that you will find it more difficult still. If a postmaster fails to deliver the notices promptly, he is subject to a fine of $50. So far as the province of Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
Prince Edward Island is concerned, I protest against that provision. I know that there will be trouble over it.
He would only have to deliver the notices in the polling subdivision once every four or five years.
Well, as he is paid only about $12 a year, if he were fined $50 and costs, he would not have much left. That is one objection, but it is not the only one. There are many other objections.

I presume that it is scarcely expected that this Bill will become law- this session. Perhaps the object of this discussion is to point out the difficulties which confront any member who undertakes to draft a Bill of this kind. A good deal has been said about the clause requiring an abstract of the law to be distributed. Allow me to read the law as it will be in that respect if this Bill passes. Section 21 will' read :
Immediately after the i^sue of the writ for election the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall transmit to the returning officer a sufficient number of copies of voters' lists and of an abstract of the offences and penalties under this Act if there are any.
It seems to me there is something very much wanting there.
The expression ' if there are any,' must have reference to voters' lists. I am afraid that is bad drafting.

I think the attention of the Minister of Justice should be drawn to this. With reference to the distribution in Prince Edward Island, it seems to me there should be no difficulty at all. The abstract is to be given to the elector by the postmaster. But I would draw the attention of the promoter of the Bill to another difficulty, which may, however, be arranged. In the province of Manitoba the post office addresses of the electors are not given in the lists, and consequently it would be impracticable there to deliver these documents through the post.

It is surprising what an amount of trouble we can surround ourselves with in dealing with matters of this kind. It would be much better to direct our attention to removing any objections that appear in this Bill, so as to make it practicable and useful. To give the notices out on the day of election appears to me to be most absurd. If you want to have information given to the electors, it should be in their possession for at least a week before. This Bill has been prepared by some of the ablest and best minds in the House, who have devoted a great deal of time and attention to it, and I do not see any reason why it cannot be put into operation even this session.

I agree with those who claim that it is very desirable that the electors should be made acquainted with the election law. To do this will entail a certain amount of expense, which I claim should be paid out of the revenue of the country. To my mind the best way of distributing this information is to have it printed at Ottawa, where it would be printed in yery large quantities, and therefore more cheaply than it could be in each constituency. These extracts could be printed here, placed in envelopes by clerks, and held here in readiness until the election. I understand that the lists used throughout the country are printed here, and these envelopes could be addressed from here to the electors, at any rate, in those parts of the country where the addresses of the electors are given. In this way a considerable saving' in the expense could be effected. Special provision would of course have to be made for constituencies in the North-west and Prince Edward Island, where there are no voters' lists.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 7 :
Subsection 8 of section 96 of the said Act is repealed, and the following substituted therefor :-
Any person who violates any of the provisions of this section shall be disfranchised for a period of seven years and shall be guilty of an indictable offence, and shall be liable, if he is a returning officer, election clerk, deputy returning officer, poll clerk or other officer engaged at the election, to imprisonment without the alternative of a fine, for a term not exceeding twelve months and not less than six months, with or without hard labour, and if he is any other person, to a fine of not less than one hundred dollars and costs and not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, or, in default of payment of such fines and costs, to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months and not less than three months, with or without hard labour.

I think it is well worth the consideration of the committee whether a clause of this kind should be adopted, when so many of the previous clauses, which involve important principles, have not been approved. It tvould appear to me also that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) *is entitled to a great deal of weight. We have before us some novel propositions, involving principles which are not, judging by the discussion so far, agreed upon ; and I am bound to say that in my opinion, even if we should affirm these principles, there is scarcely a clause of this Bill which will not require important amendment in order that it may adequately give effect to the objects we are seeking to attain. We are told that the Bill has been very carefully considered by some of the ablest men of this House, who are on the special committee. I am afraid that these gentlemen have not given it as close attention as it required, or perhaps as it has been alleged they have given 426
it, because the legislation-I say it with all due respect-is in many respects very lame and weak indeed, and in some very unmeaning. Why should the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), at this period of the session, ask the House to revise work of such an extensive character, Involving so many considerations, and which has to be dealt with by experienced persons ? In my view, it would be only fair that the committee should be asked to rise and let the Bill stand over for further consideration. There are some features of this measure which ought not to pass, and which I am prepared to oppose as far as I can ; and everybody knows that opposition at this period must be fatal. I would have preferred myself that a general discussion had taken place on the general statement of the hon. member for North Norfolk. Then we would have had the views of the various members of the committee ; and if, at a later period, this question should be taken up again, we would be able to profit by the discussion which has taken place.

If the condition of affairs in this country is as was stated by the hon. Minister of Finance, when he made the motion for this committee, I do not think that we should delay passing this Bill if we have to remain here six weeks or two months longer. I do not see that the fact that we are now in the seventh month of the session is any justification for delaying an important measure of this kind. It is not too late to pass a law, and this law, or some similar law7, if the statements of the hon. Minister of Finance are to be believed, is most absolutely necessary. It is true that we have been here nearly seven months, and that the special committee appointed to deal with this Bill has made some delay in reporting it, and it is also true that for some weeks no steps were taken by the government to place it on the Order paper ; but even as it is, I think the time of the House could not be better employed than in dealing with the election law, and endeavouring to have our elections conducted on a purer basis and with less scandal than during several years past.

I must say while no member of this House admires more thoroughly the devotion to duty shown by the hon. the lender of the opposition, I cannot enthuse over his proposition to still further delay this session possibly three or four weeks for the purpose of discussing this or any other Bill. In this case he is right in theory, but I cannot agree that he is right in practice. Members of parliament are only human, and, speaking for myself and others, we do not belong to the leisured class. We have to either divide our parliamentary duties with our personal duties, or give up the one or the other. This session has lasted so long that it has come practically to be a question with some of us whether we



*Shall give up our business or our parliamentary duties. I do not think that it would be for the good of this country that men of business should be debarred from taking part in its legislation, but that is what it will amount to if the session is further prolonged. True, the legislation is important, but there is a great deal of other important legislation that will necessarily have to be done some time in the future. We do not do everything to-day in any line of life or business. We have been here nearly seven months ; and while I have no desire to become controversial and indicate Who is to blame, the conviction as to who are to blame is very deeply imprinted in my -mind, and I am looking in the direction of the offenders. But at the risk of being controversial, I propose to say this, that an opposition which can keep this House in session, through the efforts of some seven to fourteen members, week in and week out, is not doing its duty by the country in still further declaring its willingness to keep the House still longer in session.

As far as any delay is attributable to the opposition, I think they have a very clear conscience. There has not 'been any disposition on our part to unduly protract the session. A measure of the very highest importance was brought down by the Prime Minister on the 30th of July, after the House had been in session nearly five monthe, and since that time we have been mainly occupied discussing that measure. And outside of one evening, when some difficulty arose between gentlemen on the opposite side, I believe there has never been one hour of the discussion wasted, from the standpoint of fair, honest criticism. If that measure had been introduced at the beginning of the session the time occupied in this discussion would have been regarded as extremely moderate.
What about the time in which the House was busy dis-1 cussing something else ?
What else ?
The estimates, for instance. We spent four months discussing the estimates.

And the estimates amount to about $70,000,000. And I think that, if we contrast the time that was taken up in discussing those estimates with the time taken up years ago in discussing estimates amounting to about half as much, even my right hon. friend must come to the conclusion that no undue time has been occupied in dealing with the estimates this session. I do not pretend to any extreme devotion to duty, nor do I claim for a moment to belong to any leisured class. If my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) referred to me
I certainly did not.
Whom did the hon. member refer to ?
The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane).

I may say to my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that I think I have been absent from my home and business a good deal longer than he has. I have not seen my home -since the 20th of Februray last-a week and a few days less than eight months of absence. Well, I am willing to remain even longer, if necessary, to put through legislation which I regard as of very great importance to this country. And I would not claim to be exhibiting any great devotion to duty by offering to take that course.

There are evidently many clauses in the Bill that will have to be reca-st. What I suggest-and I think it will be the sense of the committee- is to go on with the Bill and see how far we can agree. And when we have seen the points involved in each clause, perhaps we can come to a better understanding.

I think it is a pity that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) was not named a member of the committee on this Bill. As one of the law officers of the Crown, he is responsible in great measure tor the form in which legislation comes to the House. As some of the paragraphs do not seem to meet his view-and I think, perhaps his view is in some instances correct- it is not too late for him to devote time to the consideration of the ideas that are sought to be expressed, and put them in shape to be laid before the committee.

I desire to say, iu explanation, that, if in my remarks I was understood to make allusion direct or indirect to the leader of the opposition as a member of a leisured class, or to say anything suggesting a failure on his part in attendance upon his duties or willingness to do his duty, I beg to say that such was not my intention. Nobody-even in his own party- honours the leader of the opposition more than I do for his ability, shown in his profession, and his devotion to his duties, shown as a member of parliament and the leader of a party. But what I do want to point out, and what I take the liberty of emphasizing, if I may have that liberty, is that when he -speaks of his willingness to stay here three weeks to pa-ss this legislation, he speaks on behalf of from ten to fourteen of his followers, and not on behalf of the party he leads.

When this Bill was referred to the committee, it was suggested by the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that I should be a member of that committee. Unfortunately, I was engaged in arduous duties con-

nected with the redistribution, and I did not think I could be an effective member of both committees. 1 have, however, gone . over the Bill very carefully, have prepared a memorandum on every clause, and have formed my own conclusions with respect to all the clauses. 1 was anxious to hear what the members of the committee had to say before I expressed any opinion whatever oh the Bill. 1 may say that, in my opinion, with the exception of two clauses in the Bill-clause 2, which relates to compulsory voting, and clause 9-the Bill might be amended in such a way as to be of some value in connection with the Election Act. But to the first of these clauses, clause 2, relating to compulsory voting, I am opposed. I am absolutely opposed to anything in the Bill designed to make the exercise of the franchise compulsory-I am opposed to that on principle. Now, with respect to the other clause, clause 9, that seems to be absolutely unnecessary In view of the Canada Evidence Act, for that Act contains provisions of general application that meet the ease much more effectively than the clause here proposed.

As to clause 2, that relating to compulsory voting, I would point out the difficulty at which that clause is aimed. There are many people in this country who do not vote. They may be broadly divided into two classes. There are those who are indifferent, who do not take enough interest in public affairs to vote. The other class comprises those who, probably for corrupt reasons, do not go to the poll. There may be a few outside of these two classes, but, broadly speaking, these two comprise the people who do not vote. You may talk as much as you like about conscience and duty, about having control of one's duty and one's privilege. But when you bring it down to the real conditions that we have in practice, it amounts to what I have stated. Well, how are you going to deal with these men who do not vote ? It is desirable that the indifferent should have some stimulant to cause them to take part in the public life of the country. Our institutions are based upon the idea of representative government, government by the people ; and it is undoubtedly an evil if any portion of the people, from mere indifference, refuse to discharge the duties of citizenship which the law imposes upon them. Then, we have the other class to which I have referred, those people who from corrupt motives do not go to the poll. There ought to be some means, by legislation, of reaching at least some of these people ; and1 I cannot see any better way than the way suggested by wlrat I understand to have been a very large majority of the committee. If a better way is suggested, I am willing to consider it; but until that better way is suggested, I am prepared to advocate this. I have an open mind as to the best course to be taken, 426*
but I am clear that something should be done, and that we should not leave untouched the condition of affairs that exists at this time. In parliamentary elections some times not half the vote is polled. We know that death, absence, illness^ and sometimes other causes may account for some of the absentees ; but, even allowing for these, there is a very large portion of the people who do not go to the poll and vote, and it seems to me that legislation of some kind ought to be devised by this parliament to meet that condition.

But my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) must not forget that we are practically groping in the dark in proposing such legislation as this. There is no such law in existence, as far as I know, except in Belgium. It has been brought in under the new constitution of Belgium, and I am not quite sure that it has been found to work very effectively. I do not like to make a new departure without having thought the matter out very carefully. Such new departures should receive careful attention and should be seriously thought out and discussed. I have had occasion to look into the books dealing witli such questions. For instance, there is the work of Mr. Lecky, on * Democracy and Liberty,' which does not favour the principle. There is an article in the ' Forum,' on the same subject. As my hon. friend, no doubt, would like to read it, I give the reference-vol. 14, page 176. I have not been able-one simply cannot with the limited time at one's disposal during the session of parliament-come to a very satisfactory conclusion on matters of this sort. I am not sure that in a country where we have constitutional government and the people are divided into two political parties, as Is the case to-day in Canada, that if I did not belong to a political party I should be obliged to go to the poll and, because two men happen to have been selected by my neighbours, vote for one or other of them. I may not want to vote for either. I may have conscientious objections to both.
What is to hinder you putting in a blank ballot ?

If we come down to abstract theories of citizenship as a

privilege, whether in this country or in any other, it is certainly a privilege which involves responsibilities. Some of those responsibilities are imposed compulsorily. For example, the obligation of taking up arms in defence of one's country is one of the responsibilities of citizenship, and I do not know that we go any further in saying that a man is under obligation to vote at elections if he is entitled so to do by law. I read Mr. Lecky's book some years ago. It takes rather a pessimistic view of the success of representative institutions. I do not think the condition of affairs in the countries which have parliamentary government is quite so bad as Mr. Lecky is inclined to imagine. I think he has looked on the worst side of democracy in the English speaking countries at least. Further than that, if I am not mistaken, when he was elected to parliament shortly after the publication of that book, he enunciated certain views in parliament which were not in accordance with the views promulgated In the volume to which my hon. friend refers. Now I do not minimize for a moment the objections which hon. gentlemen, more especially those on the other side of the House, have urged against this principle. I know that some of them have devoted a good deal of thought to this question. But I want them on the other hand to look at the conditions we have to face, and to ask them to say in all candor whether they do not thing that there is some reason why we should endeavour to apply legislation to these conditions. It seems to me there is grave reason why we should do so. I could not express the condition better than by repeating, if it were not taking up too much time, the language of the Minister of Finance when he spoke on this question before this committee was appointed. I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, when he comes to consider the clauses of this Bill, to see whether he cannot devise some legislation, either in the form of section 2 or in some other form, which will meet the unfortunate condition of affairs to which I have referred. It is beyond doubt, as hon. gentlemen have pointed out, that the power to bribe an elector to remain at home and not to cast his vote at all, is one which lends itself to a great extent to the continuance of corruption in this country. If an elector goes to the poll you cannot, except by means of certain fraudulent devices, or by means of some connivance on the part of the officers, tell how he votes. But if that man remains at home you know he has not voted. If he is a man who is likely to vote for a particular candidate,, then by bribing him to remain at home, you make sure that that vote has not been cast against the candidate for whom this act is done. So the fact that electors are permitted with impunity to refrain from voting, helps or lends itself to a continuance of corruption, which I think demands the intervention of this parliament.

In this very clause the evil which we seek to deal with is practically sanctioned by this Bill. For Instance, if an elector desires to stay at home, all he has to do is to absent himself from the electoral district, and he remains scot free.

It appears to me that there is a want .of harmony between the argument which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) presents, and the object which he seeks to attain. The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) threw out this morning a hint which struck me at the time as a powerful condemnation of that feature of this Bill. Now the hon. member for Halifax contends there is a duty resting upon every citizen of this country to exercise his franchise, and that that duty is of so paramount a character that the law ought to be appealed to in order to compel him to discharge that duty. Well, then my hon. friend comes to parliament for that purpose, and because there may be some influences existing which may affect the result of the elections improperly and corruptly. he asks parliament to say by legislation that you Shall prolong and emphasize that evil condition of affairs ; that is to say, that while it 'is a grievous injury to the state, if a citizen does not always feel it his duty to exercise his franchise, still if he fails in one instance to exercise his franchise, he shall be prevented from exercising it at all times during a certain number of years. If it is of such vital importance that every citizen should see his duty in that light we ought rather to remove the obstacles in the way of his exercising that right in the future than to create them. We should seek to compel him to exercise his franchise then by some other method than to say : You shall exercise your franchise and if you do not we will not allow you to exercise it. I cannot see any harmony between the argument upon which my hon. friend bases the necessity for this legislation and the legislation itself. . It is an unpleasant thing for any man to take any exception at all to legislation that is promoted for the purpose of putting down alleged corruption, and I have no doubt the actual corruption, which exists to a great extent in our country. No one likes to do it because I think I am not overstating the case when I say that the great majority of public men would like to see measures passed which would prevent the continuance of this condition of affairs. If you could give us some proposed means by
which corruption could be prevented in this country I think there would not be a discordant voice in regard to it, but that all members of this House would be in its favour. But we know that as long as human conditions, human inclinations and human passions are as they are you can place all the obstacles you like in the way of these things and they will still continue. You can legislate session after session but some method will be found whereby the legislation will .be evaded. You cannot bring about a perfect condition. You cannot prevent men from running risks who are sordid and degraded in their inclinations and no penalties that you can impose will achieve any such result. But you are running a risk, if you start in upon a proposition that is made simply in the hope that it will promote the purity of elections in the country without examination and consideration, of doing more harm than good while you are absolutely failing to accomplish the purpose that you have in view. Coming to this particular clause that we have before us I may say that I do not believe it is possible to compel people who do not want to vote to go to the poll and vote. You cannot compel them. They can go to the poll, acting the part of frauds, and they can put in a ballot which is not a vote. But my hon. friend says :	Look at the frightful conditions
which result from the possibility of men remaining aw'ay from the poll and declining to exercise their franchise, what opportunities it affords for the use of those corrupt practises. But, let me ask my hon. friend this :	Has he knowledge-and he has run
elections-of the existence of any such corruption .to any very large extent or to even any extent ? I have run as many elections os any man in this House and I cannot at this moment call to mind any considerable number of instances, nor can I call to mind any occasion which I was able to say that a great many people abstained from voting because corrupt means had been employed. They abstained from voting perhaps for fear of offending somebody or for some reason of that sort, but the buying of men to stay at home has not been very generally resorted to. as a means of exercising a corrupt influence. Even granting that it was a proper remedy. We have no very considerable evidence of the existence of corruption of that character to any great extent. How are you going to prevent corruption by that means ? It strikes me that men who are open to influences of that sort will be likely to go to the poll if compelled to. accept the bribe and pocket the benefits. I do not think you are going to stop corruption by any such expedient as that. This is only a theory, as the hon. Minister of Justice says, and his view corresponds with the result of my own examination of the subject, this is a theory that has not been applied anywhere for a

sufficient time to enable us from our experience of it to judge as to whether it will be effective in any such direction.

Is my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) not aware that a good deal ott the corruption exists in hiring rigs to take electors to the polls and would compulsory voting not be the means of doing away with that means of corruption to a large extent ?

While I do believe that there Is a great deal of money improperly spent at elections I am not one of those who believe that the money spent exercises any marked influence upon the electorate of the country. I do not believe that a very large percentage of the electors of this country, while they will accept money when they see it is going, will vote differently from the way they would have voted if there had not been a dollar placed in their hands.
I quite agree if the same amount is used by both sides. If the same amount is used it does not make a bit of difference.
Does the hou. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) not know that it does not require a very large percentage in most of the constituencies in Canada to control the election ?

I will grant that it does not require a very large percentage where the parties are so equally divided. There is one remarkable fact that I think must have come home to the knowledge of every man who has been contesting elections in this country and that is that the careful canvasses that are made before the elections take place almost always are borne out by the results when the votes are counted. I know that In my own province I have seen calculations based on the result of the work of the canvassers and it has been perfectly amazing to see how accurately these calculations were made. If that is the fact what does it prove ? It proves that many influences which are exercised are vainly or ineffectively used and I do not think the case has been or can be made out to the great extent to which some lion, gentlemen think it has been made out or to an extent which calls upon us to adopt an entirely new iheory untried and unknown and the application of which would be to put a man who innocently, who for good reasons to his own conscience and interpreting his own sense of duty to his country, abstained from going to the poll on the same footing as a corrupt individual who had remained away because he had been paid to do so. To deprive him of hia franchise for six years who is innocent, absolutely innocent, mark me, and you cannot discriminate between the two, and to put him on the same basis as the other is to act in defiance of all principles of fair-play and I am decidedly opposed to the principle of the clause. While I am op-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.	'
posed to it I want to say with all sincerity that I am prepared to aid and support in any way in my power, any legislation which I believe would be effective to prevent spread of corruption or its continuation to the extent that now exists. But I will not vote for what I think would do more harm than good, for a clause which is indefensible or for measures which I am satisfied would be wholly inadequate and ineffective if passed. Like every man In this House I am entitled to exercise my judgment as to the efficacy of the remedies suggested, without being subject to the implication that I am not in sympathy with every proper and legitimate and honest means to put down what corruption does exist in the elections of this country.

There is one point upon which perhaps, the committee have not been very happy in the' discharge of their duties, although in the main they have done much good work. I can praise them in this way the more readily because although I am a member of the committee I was not able to be at any of the meetings except the initial meetings and was not present when the Bill was drafted. However, as a member of the committee I take my full share of the responsibility for its actions. I think they were not happy when they described the clause as one for compulsory voting. They thereby antagonized many persons who on a fair consideration may have been disposed to support this principle. It is not compulsory voting in the ordinary sense of the word. I can well understand a man not being willing to have a penalty of fine or imprisonment in connection with compulsory voting, but the clause in this Bill is so mildly worded that it does not seem open to as broad criticism as it would otherwise receive. It is advanced legislation it is true, but we should not shirk from legislation because it is advanced. I do not think it is open to as much criticism and objection as has been raised by some hon. gentlemen. As to the general manner in which the Bill was drafted, there is one remark which I am led to make by my regard for the chair-. man of that committee (Mr. Charlton). It would be supposed from the criticisms offered that this Bill is very badly drafted. If that is the fact we had better withdraw it from the present committee and refer it to a committee of laymen headed by the hon. gentleman from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) because this Bill was drafted by a committee composed chiefly of members of the legal profession. They were eminent lawyers, and being wise lawyers they realized that they did not know all about it-it is the man who does not know anything who thinks he knows ail-but these gentlemen knew enough to know that they did not know all and they sent to the Department of Justice for the assistance of one of the officials of that department. So you will see that

if this Bill is not all that it should be in the matter of drafting, it is certainly not for want of good legal advice.

You must not forget that after all the Department of Justice is only there for the purpose of giving effect to the instructions received. The gentleman from the Department of Justice-
I have his notes here-simply had to give effect to the instructions received from the gentlemen of the committee. I had no connection with this compulsory voting, hut I think the Minister of Finance had something to say about it.
I am quite responsible, but I never saw the Bill.

If clause 2 is under discussion, and that clause is placed there avowedly as a means of preventing the corruption of the electorate at pr.esent existing.
I would say that the objections that I had to it before are intensified by the introduction of that idea. I did not know that the electorate of Canada was as corrupt as some bon. members seem to think. I presume they draw from their own experience. I have been before the electors for twenty years, and as far as my experience goes I have never paid a dollar directly or indirectly to secure a vote in my election, and so far-*-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen are speaking for themselves, that is their privilege, 1 am speaking for myself. I do not know of a dollar having been paid either directly or indirectly to secure votes for, and I have been almost as uniformly successful as any member of the House. Therefore, I do not know from my own experience and knowledge that there is necessity for such drastic legislation to overcome an alleged existing condition amongst the electorate of this country. I object to the implication, I say that so far as my experience goes it is not true and I do not believe it is true. If it is true, representative government in this country is a mistake; we need a despotism and not government by the electorate. In regard to the adoption of compulsory voting as a means of preventing corruption, I should say from my standpoint that what we want is an intelligent election; it is mot so much the number of men who go to the polls as it is the intelligence exercised by those who do go.
What about the intelligence of those who do not go.

I am not saying anything about their intelligence. Judging by some of the representatives in this House-I do not wish to speak for myself-I should probably say they use more intelligence by staying at home than by voting. When we undertake to compel a man to go to the polls, we do not thereby put into his mind that intelligence or that good judgment or that freedom from corrupt influences which will ensure to us that he casts an intelligent and an unbiased vote. The effect of a biased vote cast at the polls is worse than the results from the bias which compels a man to stay at home. As to the general result if you compel a man to go to the poll and provide a penalty if he does not go. The provision is drastic and unreasonable and it is -bound to meet the same fate, if embodied in legislation, as all other unreasonable legislation does meet. The present law in regard to corrupt practices at elections is an instance. It is drastic and unreasonable in its present form and as a result it is not enforced and there is corruption in elections to-day, so every one here seems to say, just as there was twenty or thirty years ago, and the results and penalties 'are avoided by the principle of saw-off. I maintain that if this provision were enacted, the penalty proposed to be enforced against those who did not go to the polls would simply be settled by the principle of saw-off and there would be no penalty enforced on any one, the law- would be in disrepute and the parliament which passed it would be discredited. The hon. member for Guysboro (Mr. Fraser) drew a comparison between the position of a member of the House and an elector in the country, and he said it would not be very satisfactory to have a 'law which would compel members of parliament to vote on every occasion and that therefore it was mot desire-able to have a law which will compel electors to vote on every occasion. His argument was good as far as it went, but it was hardly fair because the conditions as between members of parliament and those who elect them are not the same in the matter of voting. A member of parliament is elected for the purpose of voting. He assumes an obligation when he stands for election in regard to that vote.
Is not the elector created for the same purpose ?

No ; an elector is not created for the same purpose. The vote is a privilege, if you like ; it is a duty, if you like ; but it should not be a penalty, as it is proposed to be made by this Bill. The true condition is absolutely reversed when you provide that the privilege of voting shall become a penalty which shall be attached to the qualification of voting.
What is the penalty ?
It is disfranchisement for six years.
Is that a penalty for the man who does not want to vote ?

Yes ; the penalty is an extreme penalty, and is improperly applied. The sufferer from that penalty is the general electorate more than the individual ; and the same fault is to be found with the

present election law ; that is to say, instead of the -man who casts a corrupt vote [DOT]being punished, it is the electorate generally who are punished. In this case Mr. A is disfranchised for six years because, for one reason or another, he did not cast his vote, and the general electorate of the country is at the loss of the weight of his influence and opinion for six years in consequence. This is putting the punishment on the wrong shoulders. But in regard to members of parliament, they are elected for the purpose of casting votes. Their business is to vote on every question that, comes up. That is the under-taking which they made with their constituents when they were elected ; and it would be the height of absurdity, it would be one of the most ridiculous things that ever occurred in the history of any couritry, it would make this parliament a laughing stock of every elector in the Dominion of Canada, if this parliament, which, on the most important question that came before' the parliament of Canada for twenty years, showed a voting strength of only, I think, 36 on one side and 74 on the other-it did not even do that, but- that is the best construction we can put upon it-if this parliament, which was not present in half its number* on that occasion, should turn around to the electorate and say : Whether you are willing or able or not, you must go to the poll and vote or you will be disfranchised. Surely we have not taken leave of, our senses altogether to put ourselves in such a position before the people who sent us here ? If the electors who sent us here are under obligations to vote for or against us at the polls, surely we are under ten thousand times greater obligations to vote for or against the measures which come up for consideration in this parliament. When we have so mended our ways, when we have so advanced, if you will call it an advance, that we have passed a law that every member of parliament shall vote on every question that comes up or be penalized, then we may discuss, with some measure of reason, a proposition that will compel the electorate to go to the polls ; but, I submit, not till then.

I have listened with great pleasure to the debate up to this time.
I think it is well to have a little mild hypocrisy in life, as long as it injures no one

The hon. member speaks for himself, I presume.
Mr. COURT,EY. And we have had not an unfair amount of it displayed in this discussion. My experience is that we have ample laws in the country at the present time to give us a perfectly pure election if the electorate and the candidates observe them. Therefore, I have listened with great amusement to this discussion, because I do not think it makes a fig of difference Mr. OLIVER.
whether we pass this law or a thousand others; it would not help the purity of elections a particle. So long as the candidates agree to suspend all ideas of morality during an election and go in for a general picnic, we shall continue to have all the expenditure of money that we have at the present time. Down in my part of the country we have the most moral people to be found in the world ; but when an election comes around, they regard it as a splendid holiday, and the result is that while the candidates agree not to spend a dollar, the electors go in for a general picnic. They size up each candidate for what they can get out of him, and they generally run it up to the limit. We might as well be honest in this matter. I will tell you of a little experience I had which sickened me of the election law. Two or three years ago I was standing at a polling place during an election of a friend of mine. By and by I saw a young man who belonged to a strong Conservative family coming across the way. I waited for him. As he came his attention was attracted by a large poster containing a proclamation setting forth all the provisions of the law forbidding any man to take a bribe or do a corrupt act. This young man, in the full flush of youth and with all the ingenuousness of youth, was coming to cast probably his first or his second vote ; and as I saw him reading this proclamation I was delighted, because I had heard men around me talking in mysterious words about * stuff,' and about not being able to get along in this election without ' stuff.' When he had finished reading the proclamation he came over to me apparently filled with the enthusiasm and purity of youth, and I expected to have a satisfactory talk with him. When he came he said : ' Who gets up all these laws about elections ? ' I immediately fell into the trap, and endeavoured to insinuate that it was the Tory party who had got them up. 1 Well,' he said,
' that is all I want of the darned Tory party. I got into a scrape the other day, and I cannot get any help from them if they make laws like this-I will go over to the Grits, who have always lots of ' stuff.' Then he went and voted. From that time T crave up any confidence in election laws.
I have listened to this debate with pleasure as an academic discussion. If the electorate do not want money spent, it will not be spent ; if they do want money spent, it will be spent in spite of all the laws you like to make. That is the honest truth in this matter.

It may be that my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) takes the proper view of the case. He informs us that laws are of no use, that yon might just as well leave the door wide open and make no attempt to control except by appealing to the individual conscience of the elector. Be a good boy and do right. How-

ever, that is not the general impression in the public. It has not been the view accepted by our law-givers in the past, and our statute-book is proof of the fact that the legislatures of this country have realized , that such an evil exists, and have tried to cope with it. Some little time ago we determined to allow section 2 to stand, and discuss the other sections of this Bill ; but the temper and disposition of the House seems to be to revert to section 2, and discuss the question of compulsory voting to the exclusion of everything else in the Bill. I had hoped that we would go through this Bill, and pass such portions of it as we consider right, and I think if the disposition of the House were to perfect this legislation, if there be anything lacking in it, we could make good progress. But the House seems disposed to question even the fundamental principles of an electoral purity, to challenge every feature of this Bill, to challenge the competency of the committee, to challenge the character of its provisions, to belittle the matter from beginning to end. This Bill, as the hon. Minister of Finance has said, was referred to a special committee, upon which were able men and eminent lawyers. As a layman and member of that committee, I can bear evidence to the truth of that statement. There were men of the most acute minds on that committee, and we had there a representative of the Department of Justice, who did not coniine his functions to registering the decisions of the committee, but participated freely in its discussions, and gave shape to the action of the committee in many essential respects. He was very conscientious and painstaking in trying to keep the committee from making mistakes or entering upon courses that would have been inconvenient, improper, unconstitutional, illegal or unw'orkable. We went on with this work to the best of our ability. The committee has presented to the House a Bill. Certain circumstances prevented that committee from making its report at as early a date as could have been desired. There was some delay iu naming the members of the committee, there was some delay in having the committee called together and organized, and what would have been a late date in an ordinary question, was reached before the committee met. But the committee did not proceed in a hasty manner with its work. It went through the work carefully in a painstaking manner. We had not the advantage of the presence of the Minister of Finance for a great length of time, but we had every valuable assistance from that gentleman. We had a representative of the Department of Justice always able to cope with the questions, and we reported a Bill which, in my opinion, requires but slight modifications, if at all, to make it workable. Many of the criticisms, I think, are not weil placed. For instance, with regard to compulsory voting, the Minister of Justice says
that the provisions of the Bill will defeat its own purpose, because a person can simply leave the riding, and thus become exempt from the provisions of the law. But the provision of the law is that if he absent himself in order to avoid voting, or left the riding for any cause not sufficient, he was liable to the consequences imposed by clause two.
Who is going to determine the reasons for his leaving V

That will be a matter to be determined on examination, like every other. With regard to the propriety of interfering with what some of our friends deem a right of conscience, which compels an individual to abstain from voting, what is the privilege of the franchise ? What is the right of the franchise ? What is the possession of the franchise ? It is the freeman's safety ; it is the freeman's weapon by which he can maintain his liberty and the free institutions bequeathed by his fathers, and which his fathers gained with great difficulties and struggles, for which men have gone to the stake, for which men have been decapitated, which has caused bloody wars and untold miseries. That is the heritage which has come down to him and which he scarcely prizes at its cost, but which it is his great duty to preserve. A great poet has said :
The crowning tact, the kingliaet act
Of freedom is a. freeman's vote.
We want to impress on the elector the gravity, the magnitude of the trust imposed on him. We want to arrest his tendency to carelessness or unconcern by saying to him : If you do not think enough of the great privilege of voting, you will be deprived of that privilege for six years. That will attract the attention of the elector to the importance of exercising the franchise. It will impress upon him the fact that this is a privilege, a great, inestimable, precious right, which he ought to exercise, and if he is so indifferent to the character of this privilege as to refuse to exercise it, in my opinion it is proper that for six years he should be debarred from exercising it, in order that he may be brought to a consciousness of its importance. And once he realizes its importance he will be careful not to commit an offence which would deprive him of that privilege. Hon. gentlemen say that voting is a discharge of a duty. Well, if a duty rests on a man. there is no impropriety in making some provision to induce him to perform it. If duty rests on a man, obligation goes with it ; and if the duty is not discharged, it is proper to impose a penalty of some kind in consequence of his failure to discharge it. If a very large majority of the electors of Canada were so indifferent to the franchise privilege as to abstain from voting, we might be governed by a minority. As

it is, with the proportion that abstains from the polls, we are not governed by the majority. There has not been an election held iii the Dominion during the last three or four years, in which the party elected had a majority of the whole electorate. A sufficient number of voters have abstained from voting to put the control of our affairs into the hands of an actual minority on the voters' lists. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Demers) says that we ought to remove the obstacles that prevent voting. That is what we are doing. One obstacle is indifference, another is the corrupt practice of hiring voters to stay at home. These are the two obstacles we want to remove, and there is no way of removing them except by the adoption of some such measure as this. The hon. gentleman tells us that if a remedy could be found, everybody would be happy. How are we to find a remedy ? If there is an evil, are we to declare that it is not proper to attempt to apply a remedy ?
Get your preachers to preach good sermons.

Preaching ? Yes, that is a good thing. I like to hear preachers preach morality and patriotism and the obligations resting upon the citizen to discharge his duty. But I like also to see his duty discharged by the citizen, and, if he does not discharge it I am in favour of applying some remedy, sonje penalty, for not having done so. The hon. member for St. John (Hon. Mr. Blair) tells us that, so far as he is aware, money does not influence elections to any great extent, that it is a matter of very small consequence, indeed, that, in fact, there is a great cry raised about this matter and very little in the cry. I cannot agree with the hon. member for St. John. I know of ridings in this Dominion that are thoroughly debauched by the use of money. I know ridings where electors have lost all sense of honour, all sense of the sacredness of the trust reposed in them, who hold their votes for sale.
Name them.
North Norfolk.
North Norfolk is a remarkably pure riding. No influences of that kind have been used in North Norfolk. But I am patriotically desirous of doing good to other ridings.
I desire, Mr. Chairman, to ask what section of the Bill we are considering at the present time ?
There seemed to be a general discussion, Mr. Chairman. I am ready to drop at once any reply to criticisms of compulsory voting if

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The opinion of the committee has been expressed two or three times that they would like a general discussion.
I understand that there is a motion that the committee rise.

That is a motion, I believe, always subject to discussion. Now, Sir, I do not think we are likely, at this stage of the session, with the temper that the House manifests, to accomplish very much with this Bill. I remember an old adage, in use among housewives when I was a boy, that the proper time to set a hen is when she is ready. The House does not seem to be ready to incubate the provisions of this Bill at the present time. That I fear is quite evident. But that being the case, while I am sincerely desirous of promoting this Bill and believe it is essential to the interests of the country that its provisions should be incorporated in our statutes, and while I believe that the Bill contains provisions that will tend very largely to correct the irregularities and corruptions that exist, perhaps it would be too much to expect to see this Bill put upon the statute-book this session. I am in the hands of the government. Through the courtesy of the leader of the government this Bill has been placed on the government Orders. Without the exercise of that courtesy it could not have been reached this session. Under these conditions, feeling that I am indebted as promoter of the Bill and chairman of the committee exclusively to the courstesy of the leader of the government, I will allow my own wishes and feelings in this matter to stand aside, if the leader of the government has any wishes or views to express as to whether we shall continue to press the Bill or be content with the general discussion we have had, and let the Bill stand over for consideration at some future period-probably another session, which, I think we are certain to have before we have another election. Of course, my own individual desire is to press the consideration of the Bill. I am ready to stay here to that end and press it to the last. It will suit me to do so. But I am not in the position to ask that that shall be done under the circumstances under which I have the privilege of discussing the Bill to-day. I am not in a position to ask that privilege from the leader of the government at this stage. Expressing my unbounded confidence in the provisions of the Bill and my sincere desire to see these provisions enacted and become law, I must realize that, in the present temper of the House, it would take some time to do that ; and 1 can do no less than return the courtesy of the leader of the government in placing the Bill on the government Orders, and leave the matter in his hands.

There are in this Bill certain dispositions with which, for my part, I altogether agree, and which I think would be very valuable parts of our law. For instance, section 8, which is the next one, we would take up ' bribery of candidates,' ' bribery of employees by employ-

ers,' ' bribery by an officer of Canada, or any province'-all these, I think, are provisions as to which there can be no objection and that would improve the law. There can be no contention, possible, so far as I can see. with regard to some of these sections. The only part as to which there is a difference of opinion-and it seems to be; a very radical difference of opinion-is as. to what has been called and has even been called in the Bill, ' compulsory voting.' It has been remarked that this expression ' compulsory voting,' is not, perhaps, very accurate. What is proposed here is not, perhaps, compulsory voting, as we have understood it here, but, even this rather lenient disposition seems to be the subject of a very radical difference of opinion, not as between the two sides of the House, but as between hon. gentlemen on either side. We have had a very valuable discussion, and tire time has not been lost. I would move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again. And I would ask the Minister of Justice to give this matter his attention, so as to keep the clauses which we think ought to be part of the Bill. Then, with regard to the second section, which is the most contentious one, perhaps we can think it over and have a further discussion upon it at a later day.

I think that would be the best course for the committee to adopt. And, in this connection, I would make one Or two further observations with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John (Hon. Mr. Blair). That hon. gentleman seems to think that this Bill excludes from voting for all time those who do not see fit to exercise the right of voting. While this Bill is intended as a deterrent. it is not intended to take away the right of voting from the people as a general rule. It is thought, rightly or wrongly, by those who have framed the provision that the very fact that a man will lose his right to vote unless he exercises that right, will cause him to go to the poll. The observations of my hon. friend from St. John seem to be illogical in that regard. He made some reflections upon the gentlemen responsible for the drafting of the Bill. I think these gentlemen have done their duty very well, it would be impossible in the time at their disposal, to frame a Bill that would not be open to criticism. But my hon. friend from St. John and any members of the government who criticise this drafting may recall the fact that the railwray commission Bill was, in the first place, drafted by a gentleman who was paid $2,500 for his work, and it then underwent Ihe supervision of the law clerks of the Department of Railways and Canals. Yet, in Committee of the Whole there were 1,500 or 2,000 amendments made in it, besides a number made in the Senate. Had the hon. member thought of this, surely he would not have found fault, because the Bill now before us requires a few
amendments. I desire to make an observation with regard to what the hon. member t'or Alberta (Mr. Oliver) suggested. He suggested that the hon. gentlemen who desired to see a law passed against corruption were making a charge against the electors of Canada. He seems to have been singularly free from any knowledge of conditions of that kind. The hon. gentleman is very fortunate. Without the slightest intention of saying anything offensive to the hon. gentleman, I may remind him of the words of the poet, ' The Lady doth protest too much, methinks.' Be that as it may, we are not making a charge against the electors of Canada by seeking to make provisions of this kind. Provisions for this purpose are already on the statute-book.
AVhen we pass laws against murder, we do not charge the people of Canada as a whole with being murderers ; when we pass laws against various indictable offences we do not charge the people of Canada with being criminals ; when we pass laws against electoral corruption we do not charge the electorate of Canada as a whole with being corrupt. Every one knows there are constituencies in which a certain number of people are capable of being influenced corruptly. In many of the constituencies I believe the number is very small, in others the number is greater. The Minister of Trade and Commerce some years ago said that in some constituencies which he named he, knew the people could be bought because he said he had bought them twice. There are testimonies of this kind found, not only in the mouths of public men, but in the court records, which show that in some constituencies there are a certain number of men who are capable of being influenced by unworthy considerations. AVhen w>e pass laws seeking to minimize conditions of that kind, we are not charging the people as a whole with being corrupt. I believe In that regard Canadians hold as high a place as any people in the world who have representative institutions such as we enjoy. There is one observation I might make with regard to what is almost a precedent for this clause 2 ; namely, that in one of the branches of this legislature a member who does not attend to his duties for two sessions, ceases to be capable of performing those duties. That is very much in line with the principle of clause 2 of the Bill. As my hon. friend from Bellecbasse (Mr. Talbot) very well pointed out while my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) was speaking, you create an electorate for the purpose of enabling them to exercise their franchise, just as you create a Senate or a House of Commons for the purpose of enabling them io perform the duties which devolve upon them. I would have been glad to see this Bill go a little further, I would have been glad to see some provision dealing with what is called ' saw-offs ' in election petitions. It is a very

simple thing to saw-off election petitions to use a common phrase; it is a simple matter, because, under the provisions of the Election Act all you have to do to get rid of a petition is to leave it for six months, do nothing with it, and the petition lapses of itself. Certain other provisions of the Act declare that you cannot withdraw a petition unless you go before a court and make an affidavit that there has been no collusion. The result is that no one goes before a court to make such an affidavit. You can get rid of it in a much easier way by not taking1, any step for six months, then the petition drops of itself. I think it would have been wise to make some amendment in that regard. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for West Elgin (Sir. Robinson) as to the appointment of deputy returning officers, I think some provision of that kind might be well included. However, as my right lion, friend says there are certain provisions about which there seems to be no great difference of opinion. These will be put into a form more acceptable to the government, and the other clauses as I understand will remain open for consideration by the House. I think that is the best course to pursue under the circumstances, and I acquiesce in his suggestion that that course be adopted.
Progress reported.
Amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 232) to amend the Manitoba Grain Act. 1900, (the Minister of the Interior) read the second time.

My hon. friend from East Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) has an amendment to make, and in order to make his amendment better understood, I will read the section which has been amended, together with the amendment made thereto by the Senate. This Is the original section of the Bill :
4. Any applicant who fails to load a car so ordered by him within twenty-four hours from the time the car is furnished by the railway company, shall lose his right so far as concerns that car ; and the railway agent shall thereupon cancel the order, by writing the word ' cancelled ' in the remarks column of the car order book, and award the. car to the next applicant entitled to it. If the applicant fails or is unable to commence loading a car awarded to him within the twenty-four hours specified herein, he shall, personally or by agent duly appointed in writing, so notify the railway agent in writing, who shall thereupon cancel the order in like manner as aforesaid, and award the car to the next applicant entitled to it. Any applicant who fails to so notify the agent as herein directed shall pay car rental at the rate of twenty-five cents per hour for each hour that the car is held for him by the railway agent, and the railway Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
company may decline to furnish further cars to such applicant until such car rental is paid to the railway agent.
That is to say, that the Bill which passed this House provided that If an applicaut failed to avail himself of his privilege, he should lose his turn and pay a penalty. This was amended by the Senate, which struck out the section and substituted the following :
4.
