Each applicant, or an agent of the applicant duly appointed in writing (such agent to be a resident in the vicinity of the shipping point), on being informed by the railway a eat of the allotment to him of a car, in good order and condition, shall at once declare his intention and ability to load the said car within the next ensuing twenty-four hours.
In the event of such applicant being unable to so declare his intention and ability to load the car allotted to him, the railway agent shall thereupon cancel the order by writing the word ' cancelled ' in the' remarks column of the car order book, and shall a-ward the car to the next applicant entitled to it.
If the applicant, after declaring his intention to load the car, fails to commence loading such car within the twenty-four hours aforesaid, the agent shall thereupon cancel the order in like manner as aforesaid, and award the car to the next applicant entitled to it, and the applicant who so fails to load such car shall pay car rental at the rate of twenty-five cents (25c.) per hour for each hour that the car is held for him by the railway agent.
If the applicant, having commenced the loading of a car, is unable to complete the same within twenty-four hours as aforesaid, he shall pay car rental at the rate of twenty-five cents (25c.) per hour for each hour over the twenty-four hours aforesaid that the car is held for hiim to complete the loading. The railway company may decline to furnish further cars to such applicant until the car rental hereinbefore referred to is paid to the railway agent.
This amendment does not differ materially from the disposition of the Bill as it passed this House, but it has been put into four paragraphs. The burden of the amendment made by the Senate is to relieve the applicant who is in default of the penalty imposed upon him.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: It would seem to me to be desirable, if these amendments from the Senate are of any importance, that we should have some notice of them upon our files.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden. Halifax) will find them at page 905 of the Votes and Proceedings.
In that case it would meet to a very considerable extent what I have said, although I think it would be wise to put amendments of this character on the files in the same way as our Bills are filed.

The amendments appear in the Votes and Proceedings. The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) might be a good one

to be adopted next session ; tliat is, that these amendments should appear on the file with the Bills.

Since this amendment was made in the Senate a good deal of discussion has taken place in the city of Winnipeg and at other points in the west as to the nature of this penalty which is imposed upon the defaulter under these peculiar circumstances. I would like to point out to the House that the change we propose to make is one which we think is reasonable and right. The individual who has been notified by the agent of the railway company, either in person or by the agent who has been appointed to act for him, has to signify his intention to the railway company to make use of the car within twenty-four hours, but in that country it is quite possible that even under these circumstances, and with the best of intentions, he may be prevented from taking hold of the ear at such a time as will enable him to finish the loading of it within twenty-four hours. If he exceeds the twenty-four hours he is liable to a penalty of $6 per day. The North-west members are in unison with me in making the statement that we object that a man living at a distance from the railway station should have this heavy penalty .imposed upon him. It is a penalty largely in excess of that imposed on any person using a rail-, way car under similar circumstances. Instead of 25 cents per hour, to be in keeping with the penalty imposed on other individuals using a car under similar circumstances, it should be something like 5 cents per hour. We think, however, that if he commences within twenty-four hours to load the car and he does not succeed in loading it within twenty-four hours he should be permitted by the railway company to complete the loading, subject, to the general Railway Act of Canada in the matter of demurrage, and that the railway company) should, instead of having it provided for in this Act, fallback upon the law as laid down in the general Railway Act of Canada, without imposing this extreme penalty. We are anxious to preserve for the railway companies the full benefit of their rolling stock, but at the same time we wish to protect the interests of those who may be prevented by the intervention of Providence, by a storm or a blizzard, or by distance, from being on the ground in time to finish within the allotted period given. There are men who live twenty! miles away from a railway station. Then there is the consideration of the mail. In some places there is only a weekly, or a biweekly, or a tri-weekly mail, and these conditions might give rise to circumstances that would prevent him from being on the ground within twenty-four hours. The amendment which we propose simply contemplates leaving the matter under the general Railway Act of Canada, and we propose to strike out this penalty and allow the railway companies to apply tile general Act in reference to demurrage in all such cases.
Suppose he does not commence to load at all. what means have you for collecting the demurrage ?
If he does not commence at all he loses his car and it passes to the next applicant. His order is cancelled.
And there is no claim for demurrage 7

No ; in that case there is no demurrage. Then there is another hardship in connection with the matter. It may be said that this is not in the interests of the railway company. But we have to look at this point : Under the present condition of things, with an insufficient supply of rolling stock, many of these farmers are perhaps obliged to drive into town fifteen or twenty miles four or five times in order to secure a car. These men should be compensated for their loss of time when they are promised a car and it has not been placed on the ground, because they are sufferers to a great extent on that account. We think, under these circumstances, that where a farmer is prevented from completing his work within twenty-four hours on account of a storm or otherwise, he should not be obliged to pay such a large sum as $0 per day, when other people engaged in other businesses are only asked to pay .$1 or $2 per day. We think that the amendment which we propose is in the interest, not only of the railway companies, but of the people of the country generally. I therefore beg to move that :
The House do not agree with the amendment to subsection 4 of new section 58, in section 21 of the Bill 232 ; but do alter the subsection by striking out all the words after the words ' entitled to it,' in the ninth line, to the end of the subsection, and substitute therefor the words ' and if the applicant, after declaring his intention and ability as aforesaid, shall not have commenced loading the car within (he period of twenty-four hours from the time of the notice to himself or his agent, as herein directed, the railway agent shall thereupon cancel the order in like manner as aforesaid.
What is the demurrage now ou a car 7
From $1 to $2 per day, and in this case they propose to make it .$6 per day.

You do not object to the demurrage of $1 or .$2 per day, as provided by the Railway Act 7
'Mr. DOUGLAS. No. This amendment provides for the usual demurrage under the general Railway Act of Canada.

I rise to a point of order. A Bill lias been sent from this House to the Senate, the Senate makes am-

endments to It, and it comes down to this House. Then this House may not concur in these amendments or may move an amendment to the Bill reaffirming the same thing as was contained in the Bill which was oi'iginally sent to the Senate. Can we then introduce entirely new matter ?

I did not read very carefully the amendments or the Bill, but I understand that we passed subsection 4 of section 21 of the Bill. This subsection 4 has been struck out by the Senate, and the Bill has now come back to the House as amended. It is now proposed to accept a part of that amendment made by the Senate and that is in order.
That is the position.

Amendment agreed to.

Bill (No. 261) respecting the Pilotage District of Montreal and the Port and Pilotage District of Quebec was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
This Bill, I understand, is to divide the pilotage system between Quebec and Montreal from that between Quebec and the gulf.

It is purely and simply to put the pilotage system between Montreal and Quebec under the control of the Department of Marino and Fisheries, in accordance with the request made by the board of trade, the shipping conference, the corn exchange and the harbour commissioners themselves, who have had these pilots under their control, and also, strange to say, with the consent and at the request of the pilots themselves. The second clause of the Bill provides that the Department of Marine and Fisheries will take control of the pilotage on the Saguenay river. The pilotage on the Saguenay river is at present under the control of the harbour commissioners of Quebec. For one reason and another the harbour commissioners at Quebec have not been willing that the pilotage system on the St. Lawrence below Quebec should be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but they do not object to the department taking charge of the pilotage system on the Saguenay river, because they have not been able to grapple with the situation. During
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Frefontaine).

speechtext: the last two seasons there have been very serious accidents on that rivei', due entirely to the fact that there has been no understanding and organization between the pilots and the harbour commissioners of Quebec. Therefore, the harbour commissioners of Quebec are disposed to allow the control of these pilots to be handed over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the department will see that pilots properly qualified to pilot on the Saguenay river will be chosen for that purpose.
Why not take the control of the whole pilotage system at Quebec as well as at Montreal.

These things must all be done by degrees; we cannot do this as rapidly as we would like, we have convinced the pilots from Montreal and Quebec that they will get fair justice from the Marine and Fisheries Department, but the others are not yet satisfied that they would get such justice, and we do not intend to force them. We had better make this experiment, and if it goes on well, I have no doubt that, in view of the result, the others will come around. If they do not we will then have good reasons to force the matter, but for the present we think it is better to take half a loaf than to have nothing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Do we understand that the pilots as well as the commissioners at the city of Quebec oppose the government taking entire control ?

I submitted this proposition to the pilots, as well as the harbour commission and shipping interests of Quebec. Unfortunately, they could not come to an agreement. I think the shipping interest would have been satisfied; but in the face of the opposition of the harbour commissioners and the pilots themselves, who constiute a corporation in Quebec, they came to the conclusion that it was better to defer action. In the meantime, this is satisfactory to every one concerned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It seems to be a step in the right direction; but I am not sure that it would not have been better to wait until the whole system was ready to come under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

My kon. friend is quite mistaken. What we are doing now meets with the approval of the corporation in question, and also the approval of the British Board of Trade, who have from time to time recommended this improvement. If this is adopted I am sure that we shall be able to devise regulations which will be so satisfactory not only to the shipping trade, but to the pilots themselves, that they will be willing in a

year or two to come under the control of the department.
On section 2-Saguenay not included in port or pilotage district of Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What proportion of the pilots will that take in ?

There should not be more than three or four pilots assigned to the River Saguenay. As the corporation of pilots of Quebec and, the harbour commissioners of Quebec could not agree among themselves, the pilotage of the Saugenay river was assigned to six or ten pilots. Some of them did not know anything about the river at all, and very serious accidents happened. That is the reason they do not object to this provision, because they think that the Department of Marine and Fisheries will make the proper choice among the pilots of Quebec, and have the pilotage of the Saguenay river as safe as any other. Until about three years ago the pilotage in the Saguenay river was done by pilots who had no special knowledge, most of whom did not know how to read or write, but who. knew the river well and scarcely any accident had happened during the time they were doing the work. But the harbour commissioners of Quebec and the pilots of Quebec represented that these people were not qualified as pilots, and asked that the pilotage of the Saguenay river should be put under the control of the harbour commissioners of Quebec. This was done, and only qualified pilots now perform the duty on the Saguenay river. It is now proposed, with the consent of the harbour commissioners of Quebec and the corporation of pilots, to make regulations for the special examination of pilots for the Saguenay river. When that is done, we hope that river will be piloted very safely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Are we to understand that under a system which allowed a man who was not scientifically educated to act as a pilot, there were fewer accidents than there have been after the change took place and a scientific examination was imposed on the pilots.

To my personal knowledge, as regards Montreal, where I was on the board of harbour commissioners for four years when I had the honour of being mayor-and I think that Quebec is no better off in this respect-the examinations of the pilots are not at present what they should be; so that what we are doing now is in the right direction. We want to have the pilots well educated, both technically and generally, and we intend to have better examinations than we have had in the past. It is also our intention to have the apprentices examined before they enter upon their apprenticeship, so that they will not lose five
or six or seven years of apprenticeship and at the end be unable to pass the examination owing to bad hearing or bad eyesight or some other physical defect.
Mr.' SPROULE. I have always thought the pilots ought to be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and it seems to me that this measure will fail to accomplish as much as it would if the whole pilotage of the St. Lawrence were taken under the control of the deparment. We shall try this as an experiment, but I expect it will not be successful. I would suggest that you should take charge of the pilots from Quebec down, as well.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Really, I think we had better confine ourselves to the pilots between Quebec and Montreal for the present, and see how that works. If that experiment proves satisfactory, we may then take hold of the pilots from Quebec down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: You may find a conflict between the Quebec pilots and the Montreal pilots.
No, because they are not in the same district.

I think it will be admitted by everyone that these are points at which it is most important that the Marconi system should be established, in order to avert the shipwrecks that are occurring from year to year. There should be no hesitancy in providing sufficient money to make these

three points satisfactory to the mariner. In doing so you provide a complete guide for the fishermen in the summer time in foggy weather. Fishermen are a class who venture a very great deal. They have been very successful in moving around Sable Island. The water for a great distance around Sable Island is very shallow. At the north east there is something like thirty miles with only twenty fathoms of water, and the same condition exists at the opposite end. I certainly would urge in the strongest manner that an effort should be made to place stations at these three points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is providing for two of the places that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kauibaeh) has mentioned. These are Cape Race, which is in Newfoundland but which is in charge of the Canadian government, and Sable Island. The third place mentioned by the hon. gentleman is Cape Sable, which is sometimes confused with Sable Island but which is a long way from it. Cape Sable is the south-western point of Nova Scotia and forms a part of my own constituency. I hope that as this system is developed it will he found possible to have a station at Cape Sable, but the urgent need now is for the improvement of the St. Lawrence route and of the signalling stations on the St. Lawrence. Cape Sable and Sca-tarie, whicli have been mentioned, are good objective points but the need at these places is not so immediate as in the case of the St. Lawrence. Sable Island, though not connected with the St. Lawrence route, is a place which is particularly dangerous, and we have great difficulty in communicating with it. Sometimes in winter, vessels are wrecked there, and some weeks elapse before we can obtain any communication at all. Cases of wrecks have occurred in which a long time has elapsed before any knowledge of the wreck reached the mainland. The situation is so dangerous at certain seasons of the year that steamers are unwilling to approach the shore. Even the government vessels have to lie off and on waiting a favourable opportunity of landing. If there is any place where this system should be established I think it is Sable Island and I am very glad to know that even though the hon. minister is not providing at present for Scatarie and Cape Sable he is providing for the other points where the need is the greatest. The others. I am sure, will come in due course.

I am very glad to hear the hon. Minister of Finance express himself in tlie way he does. I think it is in keeping for me to make a reference to Newfoundland. Newfoundland should be very grateful to Canada for the efforts she -Canada-has put forward'from year to year in providing aids to navigation in the 1 way of lighthouses, fog horns, and fog

trumpets for the guidance of vessels around that island. In the past Newfoundland has not been as grateful as she might have been towards her sister colony, Canada. It is known that although we spend a large amount of money in keeping up these lighthouses on the island for the benefit of shipping, not particularly our own but for other shipping as well, we do not get that adequate return from Newfoundland which we should have. I will refer to it here and perhaps I will in a day or two refer to it at greater length. Our fishermen are compelled to pay heavy light dues in Newfoundland ports while they come iuto our ports and pay nothing except twenty-five cents for entry and clearance. They even charge us a duty on barrels. When our fishermen tak,e empty barrels for fish, not landing them but returned to the port from which they took their departure, they charge them a duty of twenty-four cents each. This I consider an iniquitous thing.
In the event of Sable Island being connected with the Nova Scotia shore where would the station be-at Halifax V
At Halifax.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In the event of a large passenger steamer going ashore on the island with a large number of passengers there will be no accommodation and it will be of the utmost advantage that the Nova Scotia shore could be communicated with immediately.

I do not wish to undertake to speak as an expert, but living down by the ocean and like most maritime men being more or less acquainted with the wrecks that occur on our coast, I endorse what the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kauibaeh) says as to the very great importance of having one of these stations placed at the entrance to the Bay of Fundy. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Intercolonial Railway have made the port of Sr. .Tohn the Canadian winter port for the purpose cf the heavy freight traffic, and the steamers of the North Atlantic trade that come to Canada during the winter come into [DOT]St. John. We know that that locality during the last three or four years has become uri-enviably notorious for wracks. We have had a great many wrecks there and if by establishing one of these stations at this point we can do anything to reduce the number of wrecks, I think we might ask the hon. minister to consider the matter at once and to make provision for one of these stations at that port.
Steamboat inspection. $8,000.

It has been reported to me that the work has so increased in the Toronto district that a boiler inspector re-

quires to be appointed there immediately. For a number of years attention has been called to the very small salaries paid to Inspectors, a number of whom were receiving less than engineers. It is proposed to have another inspector in Quebec. Out of this amount of $6,000, the salary of two inspectors, one in the Quebec district and one at Collingwood will be provided, and in addition to that I intend to look into the salary of each inspector now on the staff. I may say candidly to the members of the committee that some of the inspectors have tendered their resignations, because they thought that if they were to engage as steamboat engineers they would get better salaries than what they are getting from the department. As they were good officials, most of them were appointed by my immediate predecessors, who had done their duty carefully, I thought they deserved to be paid on the same scale as other men of equal ability would be treated, even if they were employed by the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What salaries do they get now ?

The salaries range from $1,900, which is paid the chairman of the board, down to $1,000 per year. The majority receive from $1,100 to $1,200 per year. This inspection service has been the source of a handsome revenue to this country, but the government has decided, during this session, that the inspection fees should be abolished. The revenue which we collected from steamboat inspection amounted to $38,000, and the total expenditure was about $27,000. The services will still 'have t' be performed, but the fees have been abolished along with the tolls on the canals, because it was the unanimous opinion on both sides of the House that it would be in the interest of navigation to do so. The expenditure last year was $27,493, so that the revenue exceeded the expenditure by over $10,000. I may say that the two boiler inspectors at Toronto last year inspected 411 vessels in western Ontario. In eastern Ontario, one inspector at Kingston examined 167 vessels ; at Montreal two inspectors examined 1S3 vessels, and also inspected 430 vessels as regards tackles, loading, &c. At Quebec one inspector examined 159 vessels. He is also a hull inspector, and inspects at Montreal as well. In Prince Edward Island one inspector examined 109 vessels, in New Brunswick one inspector examined 110 vessels, in British Columbia one inspector examined 102. in the Yukon territory 144 were examined, and in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, 105.
To investigate matters respectihg sardine, herring and oyster fisheries and coast close season, $10,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What are the objects of this investigation ?

This vote is to meet the travelling and other expenses of the five commissioners who will be engaged in visiting the various points in the Bay of Fundy during 1903-4 to study and take evidence from fishermen, packers and others in the maritime provinces in regard to the matters which are menti ned in the item. They will finally make a report and recommendations regarding the best methods of preserving tlie herring and' oyster fisheries, the best means of dealing with the waste of fish due to seals, the steps necessary to promote oyster breeding, the proper close seasons, and similar matters. 1 should say that this is not a new venture on the part of tlie present minister. For years past the Department of Marine and Fisheries have been inquiring into this matter, and I may say that if the lobster industry has been saved to this country it is owing to the work of a commission which was appointed a couple of years ago, and which made a thorough investigation and a complete study of this whole question. At the present time the lobster industry in the maritime provinces is improving very greatly and its improvement we may consider due to the methods that have been adopted in consequence of the recommendation of the commissioners, which have proved very satisfactory. We intend to do the same thing with regard to the other branches as has been done in regard to the lobster fishery.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is the object of the investigation in regard to the herring and sardine fisheries ?

To ascertain the best regulations to be adopted in regard to close seasons, &c. It is a pretty difficult question to decide, and there are only a few people who can give to the department the information which will enable the country to reap the greatest advantage from this industry.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I wish to call the attention of the minister to the condition of the fishing on the south shore of Nova Scotia. I have had letters in which it is stated that the sword fish and the dog fish have almost destroyed the fishing there; and I would ask the minister to take the matter into his consideration, and try to devise some plan by which these raiders on the fisheries may be exterminated or diminished. If something is not done, the nets and appliances of the fishermen which are put out will be destroyed. These pests seem to have multiplied at a great rate during this year, and the legitimate fishing along the coast is imperilled. Perhaps some bounty for the destruction of these pests in large numbers could be given ; or if some plan could lie devised for utilizing the oil from them in some way. it would be of great advantage to the fishermen.

1 referred to this matter a few evenings ago and was asked to allow it to remain over until the estimates for the fisheries came up. In the early part of this last winter petitions, numerously signed, were sent in asking the Minister of Marine and Fsheries to see what could be done to remove this terrible nuisance, dog fish, that is increasing in numbers every year on the deep seas. It is only some two or three years that these pests have been a menace to the deep-sea fishing. Formerly they frequented shallow water, and only the shore fishermen suffered ; but now both the shore fishermen and the deep-sea fishermen suffer inconveniences. They are really a tax on the fishermen, for they suffer the loss of their nets, head lines and other appliances. They are of the shark species which eat and destroy twine. Instead of being a tax on the fishermen, these fish could be made a source of revenue, for they are worth something like $16 a ton if utilized as a fertilizer. In the memorials or petitions sent to the government reference was made to the various ways in which they could be destroyed. Dynamite would not do, for the reason that it would destroy the other fish mingling with them in the waters. The only plan which I think would be feasible and practicable, and of benefit to the fishermen, would be to offer a bounty. It could be made a small one, and it would be some compensation to the fishermen for being deprived during a certain season of the opportunity of catching any other fish than dog fish ; and the latter could be utilized, not only as a fertilizer, but as food for cattle. Cattle are very fond of these fish when dried. The fish are thrown into pickle, as the fishermen say, and afterwards dried and put into bundles and fed to young cattle in the winter time.
Wouldn't the bones bother the cattle ?

Not a mite. They eat everything ; there is no need of separating the bone at all. The fish are chopped up by the cattle as finely as if put through a bait-cutter. A great deal of loss is also occasioned in the deep-sea fisheries by the offal or the trimmings of the fish. The fishermen will anchor in the deep seas or the grand banks or where the fish are found and will lie there for a day or two fishing, when they have to leave good fishing to get clear of their debris or garbage by throwing it overboard. As this becomes the food for the fish and impairs the fishing and polutes the water, it should be disposed of in a different way. I suggest that it could be disposed of in this manner. Let a steamer be subsidized, with bait on board, to supply the fishermen who would rendezvous on these waters, and bring in return the fresh fish that are caught and place them in cold storage for transfer to the west, which is greatly in need of , that description of fish, Mr. ROCHE (Halifax).
and the trimmings as well can be preserved in lime and sand as a fertiliser. I also suggest that the oil, which is now dried out by the action of heat, aud under a system of decomposition, which renders it worth little more than 25 cents a gallon, would, if brought in a fresh state and put through a certain process, bring $2.50 a gallon, which would be a great advantage to the fishermen. This, I think, could be accomplished by giving a bounty to a steamer which would be a medium for the supply of bait to the fishermen and also for the transmission of the freshly-caught fish to some point of shipment. For instance, Canso is one point. The fish, when caught and kept in bulk for a number of months or even weeks, suffer very considerably in quality, and are not worth as much in the market as they would be if promptly transferred by a steamer. The fishermen could then sell them fresh, and the purchaser could ship them fresh, or prepare them as shredded or boneless fish, and pack them in neat and clean boxes to be sent to any part of the world ; or they could be shipped in cold storage. I therefore urge very strongly that the system of cold storage be adopted, and that Canso be made a centre of distribution, as it is midway between Cape North and Cape Sable, and is of easy access. Then, again, we want to make the fishing a success in the maritime provinces, and we want all the encouragement we can get for the fishermen. Unless they get that encouragement their industry must necessarily suffer. This year we suffered very materially for the want of bait. Had the deep-sea fishermen been able to obtain bait they would have secured valuable returns. Instead of that many of the fishermen. I am sorry, to say, will be deprived of the valuable living they have hitherto been enjoying. The bait supply is a matter of very serious consequence, and I am satisfied that the government could aid our fishermen very considerably by assistance in the establishing a system of chemical freezers. Not only would the government thus serve the fishermen, but indirectly serve the treasury as well. Our fishermen like to live well, and when they have a good catch of fish they are prepared to live on the luxuries of the land, and would therefore consume articles on which the government would receive a large customs revenue. With regard to the dog fish, which is a menace to the whole of the fisheries. I would suggest that a bounty be given the fishermen for the capture of these fish, which are indeed a nu'sance.

How much ?
Mx-. KAULBACH. I would say $4 per ton. that would not be a very great deal, and be a benefit to all concerned.
How much would that amount to ?
It depends entirely on wlmt they capture.
What proportion would the tishermen be able to catch of dog-fish in the sea V

A large quantity. If they were to go out in the morning when the fish are plentiful, they could capture a couple of tons a day. They only last but a very short time, and everything depends on the weather. As we are on this matter, you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I refer to the lobster question. A few days ago I showed how the-lobsters were being depleted on the Canadian Atlantic as well as on the American coast. In consequence of their depletion, a shell fish, known as the ' sea urchin.' which is the favourite food of the lobster has largely increased. They have become so numerous that they cover the whole shore, which formerly was covered by a coating of vegetable matter that supplied food for the other tisli, and also gave an excellent growth of kelp or sea-weed. This kelp or sea-weed was for the shelter of small fish what a forest is for birds. It gave them shelter and protection" from the larger fish. But now kelp lias all disappeared. These shell fish or little urchins, deposit a sort of saliva which covers the whole bed of the shore and becomes petrified matter, so that no vegetable matter will grow upon it. As a result the farmer must necessarily suffer. What I would suggest is to substitute the debris from the catch of the deep-sea fishermen, being the trimmings of the fish, which could he utilized as a fertilizer, and be worth about $16 per ton. when placed in a proper position as an article of merchandise, and I would strongly recommend that the government seriously consider this matter. I feel satisfied that in coming to the rescue of the fishermen they will not only benefit the fishing, but the farming industry in the utilizing of that debris because it will then be removed from polluting the waters of the deep-sea to another sphere, so to speak, where it can be utilized as a fertilizer for the farmers, so that the farmers and fishermen may receive a benefit which otherwise they would not be the recipients of at all. Therefore E would urge very slrongly on the government to give this matter its serious consideration, but by all means I ask, what I requested some three years ago, and have been asking for every year since, that a commission be sent fo the shores of the Canadian Atlantic to investigate and see what can be done in the interest of the fishermen.

This matter is of great importance to the fishermen of Nova Scotia. We have not in Canada any sardine industry such as they have on the west coast of France. We have, it is true, what we call a sardine industry, but that is really a herring industry. You are aware of the
fact, Sir, no doubt, that the fishermen, in order to fish, must have bait, and that question of bait is one which requires to be investigated. The fishermen of Nova Scotia, particularly of St. Mary's bay and the Bay of Fundy, secure the most of their bait from Grand Manan, Campobello and Passama-quoddy bay. A very peculiar state of affairs exists there. Looking at our reports, you will see that the sardine or herring industry of Canada is a very small one, whereas as a matter of fact, the herring industry, _ which is the sardine industry referred to in this item, should be worth millions of dollars to the Dominion. But instead every dollar of that or the large portion of it goes to the United States. The herring industry of the United States is wholly in Canadian waters. To-day at Lubec, a seaport right on the American border, between New Brunswick and the United States, there are invested between one and two million dollars in machinery and factories owned by Americans for the manufacture of sardines. These sardines are caught in Canadian waters, taken over to the American shores, and there sold to the American canners. They are nothing more or less than the small herring. The sardines or small herrings canned, measure from four to six inches. Any one who has studied the herring industry knows that it takes three years for a herring to mature in order to bear young. The value of the sardines put up in these cans amounts to something like $3,000,000, from which Canada gets no benefit, except what it realizes from the sale of these small herrings which are less than three years of age.
The fishermen are sending tens of thousands of casks of herring out of Canadian waters across to the American side to be manufactured and sent throughout the world. And they are nothing more or less than the small herring which belong to us and ought to be secured as bait for our fishermen. Now, the question of bait is becoming a very serious one. If you are going to deplete the Canadian waters of bait, our fishermen cannot carry on their business. A few years ago I brought to the attention of the government the fact that our fishermen are actually prevented from buying herring in Canada by a syndicate of American canners. The ordinary price for bait is from $2 to $4 a hogshead. But certain factories in the United States wanted all the herrings that were caught. They formed a syndicate and bound the weir fishermen of New Brunswick not to sell a single hogshead of bait or herring to any one except themselves, and they would take all that were offered. The consequence was that, when one of our vessels went to get bait, the weir fisherman said he was not selling any. Why ? ' Well, I have sold it all to Mr. So and So, of Lubec. and he is going to buy all we offer ; but, if we should sell you a hogshead of

bait be would take none from us.' Therefore, though they had been offered as high as $60 a hogshead and were getting only $4 from the American canners, our vessels could not get a single hogshead of bait This is one of the conditions that the government, I am glad to see, are spending $10,000 to investigate.
These fish are caught in weirs. The government licenses these fishing sites and charges a license fee of $5 a year. I know of people living in New York who pay $5 a year license fee, and then sublet the site so secured for $2,500 a year. These websites are worth all the way from $1,000 to $4,000 a year, and they are nearly all in the possession of a few gentlemen-and I know of one lady, she being the one to whom I have just referred, ns receiving $2,500 for the sublease-who do not reside on Grand Manan or near the fisheries, who are not interested in the fisheries except as holders of these licenses, which they sublet to' parties who fish on these islands. This thing has been going on for years.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that these licenses are all held by Americans ?
Oh, no. But I do say that the parties do not reside where the weir fishing is going on.
How long is one of these licenses good for ? '

For a year, and the charge is $5 a year. Something should be done, and I am glad that the minister is investigating this matter in order that the license fee may be increased and the arrangement made different from what it is at the present time.
Now, the situation in regard to bait is becoming so acute with us that we have asked the government to erect bait freezers. I am glad lo say that the government have voted the money to erect these freezers in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. These have proved of tremendous benefit to our fishermen. We have in the province of Nova Scotia, I think, something like 40,000 men engaged in the fisheries. For a period generally of about six weeks in the summer they are unable to procure any bait at all. And, the season when this condition exists is the very best fishing season. The government, by erecting these bait freezers, have placed the fishermen in such a position that they can store bait when it is plentiful, and take it out during the season when bait cannot otherwise be procured, and so continue tlieir fishing, as they have not been able to do for some years past. The bait has to come from Grand Manan, where the sardines are caught. I congratulate the minister on deciding to have this question investigated.
The dog-fish referred to by one hon gentleman has become a serious menace to our Mr. COPP.
fisheries in Nova Scotia. If the problem is not dealt with in some way, it is going to seriously affect the fishery industry of the Dominion. I have here a copy of the Halifax ' Herald,' of October 3rd, which shows how the dog fish is helping to destroy this industry in Nova Scotia. This newspaper tells of ' Half a million shortage in our western fisheries.' ' It is estimated that west of Halifax'-that is, in the five counties of Lunenburg, Shelburne, Queen's, Yarmouth and Digb.v-1* the fishing catch is $400,000 to $600,000 below the average this year.'
It is all of that.

And this newspaper says that the dog fish and the scarcity of bait are the chief causes. If, in one year we lost in five counties a sum equal to $400,000 to $600,000 through tlie dog fish and the scarcity of bait, hon. gentlemen can see what this means to the whole fishing industry of the maritime provinces. The bait question, I am glad to say, is one with which the government is dealing. And I believe that they are dealing witli it in the right way, and in such a way that, in a short time it will be satisfactorily dealt with.
Wbnt is the size of this fish ?
From a foot to two feet in length.
W-hy are they called dog fish ?

I do not know. They are a
species of Shark. They are very pugnacious and destroy everything that comes in their way.
They are the most aggressive fish in the water.

By long odds. Formerly they visited us annually, but remained for only a week or ten days. They struck in about May and would remain in the Bay of Fundy St. Mary's Bay and adjacent waters for about a week or ten days and then would disappear. While they were with us, of course, no fishing was done. The moment they struck in. the fishermen came ashore and remained idle. Of late years they are remaining the whole year round. If they are to remain with us in the future the fishing industry will become almost a thing of the past. Last year, strange to say. they made their appearance on the banks for the first time in the history of the bank fishery.
They appeared three or four years ago.
Fourteen years ago- in 1889.
Not in any number, I think.
The suggestion I have to make is in line with that of the hon. member for

Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach). The only way in which to deal with this question of the dog fish is by a bounty from the government Whether it should be a bounty to reduction works or to the fishermen is a question we have to consider. Of course, 1 am in favour of a bounty to the fishermen. I think that a bounty direct to the fishermen would stimulate the fishermen to catch the fish, whereas, if the bounty were given to the reduction works they might take advantage of it, and the fishermen would get no | benefit from it. In the county of Digby last year. I had the representatives of a Philadelphia firm come down and they went to Tiverton and Briar Island with a view to erecting reduction works. The only thing they were afraid of was that they could not secure sufficient fish to keep the works going. They told us that if the government would agree to give a bounty on the dog fish, so that the fishermen would catch them, they would at once talk business with us j as to establishing the reduction works. If we had reduction works situated at three or four places in the province where they catch these fish and could sell them, it would be a profit to the fishermen and they would engage in that kind of fishing. As it is, dog fish does not seem to be worth anything. There is nothing we can get out of it unless we cut the liver out and extract the oil. But the oil that is taken from the fish is not sufficient to justify the fishermen in engaging in that fishery. I am going to ask the minister if it is not possible for him to add to the item now under discussion a clause that will enable the commission to investigate and report upon the dog fish nuisance. The sum of 810,000 is more than enough to pay all the expenses of investigation that is required in the Bay of Fundy, and all that is needed is to give the commissioners power to investigate the dog fish nuisance. Now, the lobster industry is referred to by the minister, and I must congratulate this government on taking that up and appointing a commission which has done this country immense benefit in the report they have made. It almost solves the lobster problem. Everyone knows that the lobster industry to-day is worth in the province of Nova Scotia alone 83,000,000, whereas thirty years ago there was nothing in it. I believe the same result in regard to dog fish can be accomplished through this commission that the minister now provides if it is properly conducted. Another thing I wish to refer to is the license taken out by American fishermen. Atnericans are taking fish in our waters, and before they can do so they have to procure a license and pay so much a ton. But they ton their vessels in the United States, and when they come to Canadian ports they pay a tonnage on the American register, that is not one-lialf as high as the Canadian register. Therefore a vessel that measures eighty tons by the Canadian register would only measure forty tons by the
American register, and when they come into Canada and take out this license to fish they purchase their license on the American register, which only shows forty tons whereas they should pay a license on our own Canadian tonnage. I think the minister should make a regulation which will compel them to pay this license on the Canadian register.
Mr. KAULBACH, I feel satisfied that it is better to give the bounty to the fishermen than to give it to reduction works. Let the bounty be given to fishermen as an inducement to them to engage in catching this fish. The reduction works can then come in and receive their profit by utilizing the dog fish as a fertilizer. The difficulty is to bring the dog fish in to shore in a proper condition to be utilized, but that difficulty can be overcome by using lime. They can take out a few barrels of lime with them, and by its use prevent the fish from decomposing or becoming offensive to the sense of smell. They can do the same with the debris that is taken from the trimmings of fish. It can be cured in such a way that it will not he offensive, and become solid matter by placing with it quantities of lime. In that way the reduction works will get the benefit in the end without any bonus being given to them by this government. But let the bounty be given as I already stated, to the fishermen directly.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What has been the expenditure so far in the Behring Sea matter V

In 1901-2 the expenditure was 82,956; last year it was only 887. The whole expenditure is somewhat between 850,000 and 860,000.
Towards providing for a steamer to replace the ' Acadia,' a,nd one to replace the ' Petrel ' on the great lakes, $75,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The Acadia was offered for sale some time ago, was she sold '!

Yes, she was sold by tender, after all her fittings had been taken out of her, anything that was of any value. There were two tenders, one for 86,050 from St. John, and one for 80,000 from Halifax, the latter of which we accepted. She was sold about two months ago.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Was any money expended on her last year ?

Yes. to repair and put her in commission, but the vessel was perfectly useless. The vessel was condemned, and none of the officers would risk their lives on her. She had been kept up from year to year by repairs, until finally she became so old and useless that we thought we would get rid of her. I think what we took out of her was worth $5,000 or $6,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I did not catch the hon. gentleman's remark with regard to the amount that was realized on her.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What about the 'Petrel ' ?

The ' Petrel ' will be put to the service of the buoys. She is not considered fit for the service which she has been doing for the last two or three years. She is not fast enough. We are the laughing stock of the Americans and our fishermen complain that she does not afford the protection that is necessary. We want to replace her with a 15 or 16 knot boat so that we can catch those Americans who are poaching in our waters.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: You are going to use her for another purpose ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Have you bought any new boats to replace these ?

No, the 'Acadia' has not been replaced. The ' Petrel ' is doing service. We are asking for $75,000, but this is only a preliminary expenditure. To replace the ' Acadia ' by a 16-knot steamer we will require from $150,000 to $175,000. We can replace the ' Petrel ' with a boat constructed in some of the ship-yards in Canada at a cost of from $50,000 to $75,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Why do you not get a turbine ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I hope we may some day.

Will the boat to replace the ' Acadia ' be of	steel ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes, and she will be armed as well.

Don't you think wood would suit as well to traverse the shore ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. No.

Then you are buying one and building the other ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. We do not intend to buy either. We intend to have the boat to replace the ' Petrel ' constructed here according to plans made by the department, and Mr. BLAIN.
for which we will get tenders from Canadian firms.
And the other ?

We will have it constructed on plans prepared by the officers of the departmen t.
Mr-. KAULBACH. Is it under the consideration of the government to grant a bounty to encourage steel ship-building in Canada ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
That has been talked of a good deal, but I am not in a position to state whether the government has considered the question or not.
Further amount required for building and maintenance of fish breeding establishments and lobster hatcheries and securing seed lobsters during the fish season for distribution, in depleted localities, $15,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has come to any decision regarding the application made last year for the establishment of a fish hatchery on the Beaver river in the county of Grey near the Georgian bay. It is in close proximity to where the fish ova are caught and would in. my judgment be a splendid place for a hatchery. I mentioned It last year to the hon. gentleman's predecessor.

We propose to establish eight new hatcheries which will be provided for out of this sum, and the one to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) makes allusion is provided for. The exact site has uot yet been decided by the department. The conditions of the place mentioned by the hon. gentleman as far as they have been ascertained by the officials entirely meet the requirements.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am sure the people of that section will be grateful for it as they have thought for a long time that this place was a very suitable one and a fish hatchery will be very useful there.
I wish to ask the hon. minister if it is the Intention to establish a hatchery in the Bay of Fundy ?
Yes. There are demands for thirteen new hatcheries, but. as I have stated, provision is made this year for. eight.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: How many are there for Lunenburg
There is one for the district combining the counties of Digby, Annapolis and Yarmouth, but the exact situation has not yet been decided on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I would ask, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. minister does not think it is fair that the county of Lunenburg should have one ? It excels any other county In the industry of fishing. We have

a number of canneries in the county and I think we certainly should have a hatchery. Would the hon. minister reconsider and give us one ?

I am not an expert in these matters, because I am a new hand at it, and when you ask me about sites for hatcheries I will have to depend a great deal on the officers of my department unless I can go myself and visit the places. It is very hard for me to fix on one place or the other unless my officials advise me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will consider the record we hold in regard to fisheries I think he will see that it warrants him in giving one at least to the county of Lunenburg. I think I have a knowledge of the matter equal to that of any commissioner or of any one else he can send to make inquiry.

I would support my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach). He has succeeded in taking the fishing industry away from Halifax to Lunenburg and it is the head centre of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia to-day. Besides, it is near the county of the hon. Minister of Finance and some benefit might overflow into Queen's But. I think in deference to the fishing industry, there should be a station in Lunenburg.

In regard to the remark of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) that Lunenburg is the centre of the fishing industry I would say that in one sense only that is correct. Lunenburg is the centre of the deep-sea fishery, but it is not the centre of the lobster fishery which is the subject under discussion. I think I represent more lobsters than any body else in this House.
We think so on this side of the House.

And I do not mean to call my constituents in all cases lobsters either. The lobster industry is a very important one in the counties that I represent. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been too modest in his statement. He has recently made some experiments in the eastern part of Nova Scotia in regard to the propagation of lobsters which have been remarkably successful, so much so that I question whether in the future it will be necessary for us to do as much in the matter of lobster hatcheries as in the past. The experiments that have recently been made by Mr. Barker at Foureliu in Richmond county have been remarkably successful.
What is the nature of them ?

It is the creation of the lobster pound into which seed lobsters purchased from the fishermen
are thrown, and then, as the Irishman says, they let nature take its course. There were no special arrangements for conserving the seed lobsters and the fishermen were very apt to destroy them. Although the law forbids that, still you cannot always enforce these laws. The action recently taken by the minister was to offer a price for the preserving of the seed lobster. That was then taken to the pond and placed under proper supervision and the development has been very remarkable. Of course this work may be said to be yet experimental, but it has been so successful that I should think that in most parts of the country they would prefer this natural development of the lobster to the creation of lobster hatcheries. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to be congratulated upon the great success that has crowned his efforts in that direction.

I have been urging that suggestion for years, the use of natural pounds where there is a flow of clear fresh salt water at every' tide. We have several of these in my county, one east of Chester- where there is now a cannery at the town of Chester-and one at the mouth of the La Have river, and both are admirably placed for the purpose. I am satisfied to allow the minister to have a claw on a portion of the claim, but I would rather not see him obtain the whole of it. I want him to be as a friend generous in this matter, and 1 think my request is reasonable, and one which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see to be in the interest of the fishermen of my county. It is right for the fishermen there to have a claim to at least a portion of such benefits. The county of Lunenburg, from Queen's to the border of Halifax county is one continuous line of ' shore fishermen, and I will ask the hon. minister to look carefully into this matter and give me at least a hatchery for one of these pounds.

I am perfectly satisfied that Lunenburg should have the credit of representing the largest fishing county in Nova Scotia, but I wish to warn him of one thing, that he has so little advantage in this respect that it is not very much to brag about. In Digby last year the total catch was $1,438,942, whereas in Lunenburg it was $1,484,000, or a difference of only $45,000 in favour of Lunenburg. I wish to draw his attention to this, that while the yield in Digby has been going forward by leaps and bounds, Lunenburg has gone behind. Therefore, unless there is a change in Lunenburg very soon, I shall have the proud distinction of representing the largest fishing county in Nova Scotia.

I can easily explain that and show very clearly the position with regard to the catch of lobsters in my county. The lobsters captured in my county are largely taken from my county into the adjoining counties of Queen's and Halifax and

are counted as a catch for these counties, when in reality Lunenburg is deserving of all that credit.
To increase the salaries of R. N. Venning, $150 ; F. H. Cunningham, $100 ; D. H. Fraser, $150 ; J. F. Fraser, $450 ; F. Anderson, $150 ; J. M. Lalonde, $150 ; C. W. White, $100 ; J. M. McCharles, $200, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,450.

Why do you require all these increases ? Have these men not been getting any increase in salary for some years ?
The ' MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. Most of them have not got the ordinary increase, some of them for four years and some of them for less. I will enumerate the different officers. Take Mr. Venning. His salary is $2,050, and this increase makes it $2,200. He joined the service in 1869, and has been strongly recommended for the maximum of $2,400 for his special services in connection with the Behring sea arbitration and other international as well as intercolonial affairs. He is one of our most capable officers in the Fisheries Department. He lias assisted at these different commissions and rendered most valuable services, and I do not know how it was that he remained at such a low salary, and it has been thought proper to increase his salary by $150. As regards Mr. Cunningham, I may say that his duties have been increased very largely. He is a first-class clerk in the department, and is also inspector of fish hatcheries throughout the Dominion, a very important and growing work, which keeps him travelling a great deal. He has perfected a device for carrying fish long distances which has been successfully employed, for instance, in stocking the waters of British Columbia with bass, where the fish were canned 2,800 miles. Ho lias been twenty years in the service in all kinds of work, in connection witli commissions and special inquiries, and I consider him deserving of the increase.
His present salary is how much ?

One thousand six hundred and fifty dollars. Mr. B. H. Fraser is a graduate and medallist of the Royal Military College and has been in the department since 18S9. He was employed in the office of the chief engineer, and in 1885 he was appointed assistant engineer in the absence of the chief engineer. I may say in regard to some of these officers, that if they were in other departments in the outside service they could get much larger salaries than they are getting, and some of them have tendered their resignations, because, as the members of the committee are perfectly aware, engineers or experts, men with a certain technical knowledge, are at present being looked for, and it is in view of this fact that I have thought proper to make Mr. KAULBACH.
these increases. Mr. J. F. Fraser is in a similar position. He has charge of all the buoys and lights on the upper St. Lawrence and the lakes, and down as far as the gulf. He is a capable engineer and we cannot really keep him at a salary of $1,550. He will leave the service if he does not receive a larger salary. He is also a medalist of the university.
Mr. Anderson is a graduate of the Royal Military College. He has been engaged in the hydrographic survey since his appointment, in October, 1893. He is receiving $1,050, anil it is proposed to place him at $1,200. He lias charge of the survey in .Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Mr. Lalonde has been receiving $850 and it is proposed to place him at the head of his class. He has been highly recommended by the deputy minister and accountant for his increase. He received no increase for years and years, and is a very capable officer in the department. He is one of those who would certainly leave the service if he did not get better remuneration for ills services. Mr. White joined the service in 1S93. Ii is proposed to increase his salary to $900. For the past year he has had very important work to do in connection with the revenue, and is a very painstaking clerk. Mr. McCharles joined the service in 1893 -and is receiving $700. It is now proposed to raise him to $900. He is a good stenographer and typewriter, and at present has charge of the work of despatching all mail matter, which was formerly done by a first-class clerk. He was strongly recommended for an increase by tlie deputy minister.
To promote Jules d'E. Clement from a second-class to a first-class clerkship, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $300.
To promote M. C. Doyle from a junior second to a second-class clerkship, $100.
To provide salary for A. M. Ross as a junior second class clerk, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $900.
To provide for the salary of F. H. Houde as a junior second-class clerk, $600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: As regards Mr. Clement, I may say that he is my private secretary. He had been in the service as private secretary to the Minister of Public Works before he became my private secretary. It is proposed to make him a first-class clerk, which is the rank of nearly every one of the private secretaries to the ministers. He writes both English and French.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What salary would that give him ?

$1,400 and the amount which is allowed to him as private secretary, $000. He is a stenographer in French and English, so that I save the salary of an English stenographer. Miss Doyle is an old employee of the department, appointed in 1892-I mean she has been employed for a long time. She is assistant private seere-

tary, being an expert stenographer, and typewriter, and I think an increase of $100 to her is not too much.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is her salary now 1

$1,000. Mr. Ross has been in charge of the fisheries museum, and has also been employed in connection with fish' breeding. It is now proposed to put him in the Inside service at a salary of $900, being the amount he now receives in the outside service. Mr. Houde is a young clerk who enters at the foot of the ladder at $000. He is a stenographer, and a useful young man.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There are two new clerks appointed, then ?

To fill vacancies. There was one pensioned and one transferred. The private secretary of the former Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Hunter, was transferred to the Department of Public Works. That is the only appointment that was made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister did not tell us when these employees got the last increase.

Mr. MeCharles was kept out of his increase for four years. Mr. Yenning was kept out of his increase for three years. Mr. Cunningham has $50 besides the regular increase. As I have stated, he is a technical officer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: How do you regard him as having technical knowledge, if he has been a clerk in the department steadily getting the regular increase ?

Mr. Cunningham is from the old country. He has special work to perform, and the experience he has acquired in the department entitles him to a larger salary. He is inspector of fish-breeding establishments, having made a special study of that branch of the work. What I say for one is applicable to the others ; that is, that these increases are either to correct an in* justice that has been done or to render justice to officials who, in any other department of the public service, would be entitled to the salaries that I have thought proper to allow them. I do not know them personally, except those with whom I come in contact, like Mr. Yenning, Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Clement. The others have been recommended by the deputy minister ; and, after considering their cases, I came to the conclusion to recommend the increases.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I do not wish to be understood as objecting to these increases ; [DOT]but I rise for the purpose of calling attention to the fact that we contended that 428
great injustice had been done to many members of the civil service for several years after the hon. gentleman's friends came in, by depriving them of the statutory increases to which they were entitled ; and now the hon. gentleman proposes to make those increases up. We have had sharp arguments on this subject in previous years, and I am glad that the ministers now recognize that they were wrong in the past. If they had followed the practice of their predecessors, it would not have been necessary to make such large increases at the present time. Most of these employees would have reached the salaries they are getting by means of the ordinary annual increases instead of getting these increases in a lump sum.
I do not cast any blame on anybody. I found the cases to be as I have stated, and I tried to deal with them to the best of my knowledge and judgment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman will not try to fix the blame on anybody, but it is our duty to fix it on the parties who are blameworthy, and that is the hon. gentleman's friends.

I would ask my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), if he considers that the Liberal party have neglected certain oflicials for- five years, what would he think of the former party, who neglected to give certain officials their statutory increases for eighteen years ?
I do not know of any such cases. I think the hon. gentleman is drawing on his imagination for his alleged facts.
I beg to correct the hon. gentleman. I can give the names of the individuals. I know them perfectly well.

Keep them till next week.

We may take up first one or two Bills which stand in the name of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and then go into Committee of Supply.
